**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 38, verse 2:**

﴿But those who disbelieve﴾: in what they display of denial of Him. ﴿Are in pride﴾: that is, in hardship, difficulty, and contention through the zeal of the *jahiliyya* (the age of ignorance before Islam). They are enveloped by it, so it blinds them to the truth because it encompasses them. He used the feminine form (*anna_tha*) to indicate its weakness and to give good news of its swift passing and its turning into humiliation. ﴿And opposition﴾: that is, turning away, refusing, and arrogance against accepting the truth, from the two tongues of circumstance, which existence has expressed clearly, and of speech, which the Remembrance has stated explicitly. He guided them to what is in their natural disposition and innate constitution, with the most elegant expression and the clearest indication, ﴿if they had understanding﴾. But they turned away from reflecting on it out of obstinacy, not conviction: ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33]. Their being indefinite (*tankir*) is for magnification. Al-Razi said: He omitted the response so that the heart may go in every direction within it, so that it may be more abundant and its seas more surging, end of quote.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When Exalted is He mentioned the condition of the earlier nations with their prophets in transgression and denial, and that this resulted in their being seized with a severe and prolonged punishment, this was an occasion for reminding of the condition of the Arab polytheists and explaining the evil of their conduct, and that they had preceded others in that offense, so the severe punishment befell the obstinate. He therefore laid out the condition of these people and the evil of their speech, so that it would be known that there is no difference between them and the deniers of the earlier nations regarding deserving punishment and the evil of their end. This was explicitly stated in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh of the stakes, denied before them﴾ [Sad: 12], up to His saying: ﴿Each of them did not do other than deny the messengers, so My punishment was justified﴾ [Sad: 14]. When Glorified is He followed this with mention of their seeking to hasten (the punishment), in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share before the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Sad: 16], He followed that with commanding His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient, saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Sad: 17]. Then He consoled him by mentioning the prophets and the condition of the near and chosen servants: ﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers that which We strengthen your heart with﴾ [Hud: 120], end of quote.

(p-325) Since the knowledge that God willed to manifest in this existence has two paths, a state (ḥāl) and a statement (maqāl): as for the state, it is that which the conditions of the existents, which He originated (ibdāʿ) in this cosmos, speak of, in the form of knowledges, of which whoever God wills to perceive perceives. As for the statement, it is this Reminder (dhikr), which is a translation (tarjamah) of the whole of existence. God, may He be exalted, had put the Reminder first, because it is clearer and more manifest; and He informed that they turned away from it and opposed it (shāqqūhu). And whoever opposes the King deserves destruction. What they displayed of contention (mughālabah) was a matter that enraged the believers, so He followed it with what is fitting for frightening the disbelievers and giving hope to the believers, through what the tongue of the state (lisān al-ḥāl) expressed, namely the destruction of those who were warned; and this is the clearest of its indications and the most manifest of its signs. So He said, as a resumption (istiʾnāf): ﴿How many a generation did We destroy﴾. It is as if those who were being addressed by what is mentioned were among some of the destroyed, and they were the nearest of the destroyed to them in time; so He introduced the preposition (jārr) for that, and said, indicating the beginning of the destruction: ﴿before them﴾; and He emphasized their multitude by His saying, as a specifier (mumayyiz): ﴿of a generation﴾; that is, they were in opposition like their opposition, because they were at the extreme of hardness, sharpness and might, as indicated by "qarn" (generation).

When their distress resulted from the touch of punishment, He said, gathering [the verb] in accordance with the sense of "qarn," because it is more indicative of the greatness of the destruction: ﴿and they cried out﴾; that is, with what was said to them: that it was a means of salvation, through faith and repentance; and they sought help from one who would rescue them; or they performed the calling out (nidāʾ) out of terror and bewilderment, without intending a person called upon; so the verb would be intransitive. Al-Kalbī said: when they fought and were compelled, they called out "manāṣ" (there is no escape), that is, "upon you is flight"; and they were answered that there is no flight for them.

Since God, may He be exalted, established in more than one place that repentance benefits only at a time of capacity and choice, not at a time of overpowering and agitation, He said (exalted is He), emphasizing this meaning in a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), by adding the tā' (whose origin is hā') to "lā," or to "ḥīn," just as they emphasized by adding it to "rubba," "thumma," the hā' in "arāqa," the tā' in "mithāl," and "al-āna"; so they said: "rubbata," "thummata," "ahrāqa," "timthāl," and "tāl-āna": ﴿And there is no time﴾; that is, the time is not ﴿for escape﴾ (manāṣ), that is, flight, by movement forward, nor backward, by a strong movement nor a weak one, let alone salvation. Ibn Burjān said: "al-nawṣ" is expressed by it sometimes as advancing and sometimes as retreating; it is like the bolting and shying of a horse; and "nawṣ ḥimār al-waḥsh" (the wild donkey's nawṣ) is its raising its head, as if it were fleeing and bolting.

(p-٣٢٧) Since making him a warner from among them was not a fitting matter for wonder, yet they treated it as wonder, because of what appeared from their dividing up their speech about him, He expressed their wonder in His words: ﴿And they wonder that﴾; that is, because of the fact that; ﴿there has come to them﴾. Since their wonder was at the mere fact of his warning and not at its intensity, He used the active participle rather than "fa'il" and said: ﴿a warner from among them﴾; that is, from among mankind, then from among the Arabs, then from among the Quraysh. He was not from among the angels, for example, and they ought not to have wondered at this. For a warner who comes from among the very people he warns, and who is also the most noble of them, is more fitting for warning, because they know him best, and know what truthfulness, compassion and other qualities he embodies. This is how custom has always worked, in the past and the present, since people incline more toward one of their own, and so they are more receptive to his words.

Since they were the people who knew this warner (ﷺ) best, in that he was the most truthful in speech and the most lofty in aspiration, and that every flaw and stain was far from him, He increased the wonder by saying, using the conjunction "wa" (and) rather than "fa" (so), because their describing him as a sorcerer is not comparable to this wonder: ﴿And said﴾. Since they were concealing the truth while knowing it, they were deniers, not ignorant; and obstinate, not heedless. He placed the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun, (p-٣٢٨) as an indication of this, and as a notice of His intense anger, in His words: ﴿The disbelievers say, "This [is]"﴾; that is, the warner.

Since what he displayed of extraordinary signs was a miraculous proof (i'jaz), both in deed and in word, which draws hearts, and since the nearest thing they could use to discredit it was sorcery, they hurled that charge at him. They did not use the form of intensive emphasis, lest that should amount to a clear display that attracts hearts to him. So they said: ﴿a sorcerer﴾; that is, because he separates a man from his wife by what he brings. Thus they acknowledged, while attributing sorcery to him, and while knowing they were lying in this, that what he brought was beyond the powers they had: ﴿a liar﴾; that is, in his claim that what he worked magic with is true, and is not like the sorcery of sorcerers. They used the intensive form shamelessly, although before this they had called him "the Trustworthy" (al-Amin), and they knew that nothing new had come to him except that he brought the utmost truthfulness and the greatest truth, together with his ascent through the stages of perfection, which is hidden from no one who gives it even a little reflection.

When he mentioned their statement, which arose from their astonishment, he mentioned its cause, so that it would be known that their own state is what deserves to be wondered at, not the state of the one who warned them. In saying, quoting their words, to deny the content of what preceded it: ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾, that is: has he turned, by reason of what he claims is revealed to him, ﴿the gods﴾, that is, those we worship, ﴿into one god﴾. Since the discussion concerns divinity, which is the greatest of the roots of religion (uṣūl al-dīn), and since he (ﷺ) and all who followed him, indeed every fair-minded person, deny that this is a wonder, but rather the utmost wonder lies in one whose reason accepts that God may be more than one, they emphasized their statement for this reason, and to inform their weak-minded followers, to reassure them that they are in the utmost certainty and conviction regarding what they say. The strange circumstances they witnessed from their warner, which necessarily indicate his truthfulness, did not shake them; so they called them sorcery, because they were unable to match them. ﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, the saying of monotheism, ﴿is truly a thing of wonder﴾, that is, in the utmost degree of wonder, by what the dammah and the form (ṣīgha) indicate. For this reason it was read anomalously (shādhdh) with the letter jīm doubled, and that is more emphatic.

The Ustadh Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī said: They did not know God, nor the meaning of divinity, for divinity is the power to originate (ikhtirā'), and assuming two beings capable of origination is not valid, because it necessitates the existence of mutual obstruction between them and its possibility; and this prevents the perfection of both. And if they were not of perfect attributes, they would not be two gods; and every matter whose establishment entails its own collapse is false and discarded. End of quotation.

The allusion to refuting them will come with His saying: ﴿the Mighty, the Bestower﴾ [Ṣ: 9], then with His saying: ﴿There is no god except Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ṣ: 65].

And since wonder, let alone extreme wonder, is worthy of clinging to its owner so that the beholder's amazement increases, he showed that they did the opposite. This confirms what he attributed to them of schism. So he said: ﴿And the chiefs went forth﴾. Since what they did is not something any sensible person would do, the listener might suppose that those who went forth among them were the base people from elsewhere. So he said: ﴿the chiefs﴾ (p-٣٣٠), i.e., the nobles, and he said: ﴿from among them﴾, i.e., not from others. How much less, then, would the base among them be included, and how much less others? Then he specified the going forth by implying speech in it, since speech is one of its requirements, with his words: ﴿saying, "Walk on"﴾. I.e., each of them said this, commanding himself and his companion to part earnestly, in conduct and in speech. When one pauses on أنْ (an), it is begun with a kasra on the hamza, because its original form is امْشِيُوا (imshīū), so the third letter is kasra, just as when a woman is told اغْزِي (ighzī), one begins with a damma, because the original is اغْزُوِي (ighzuwī), like اخْرُجِي (ikhrujī). ﴿And be steadfast for your gods﴾, i.e., in keeping to their worship and not turning to anything else. Al-Qushayri said: If the disbelievers counsel one another to be patient for their gods, then the believers are more deserving of patience in worshipping their Lord and of steadfastness in their religion.

Since each of them had taken into his heart what he heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) and it had seized his intellect, as indicated by ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder, but...﴾, and since he feared his companion might have turned away from belief in the One God because of what he knew of his wavering within himself, they emphasized their saying: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, i.e., patience in the worship of the gods, ﴿is surely a thing that is intended﴾, i.e., it is worthy of being intended, and so it is worthy not to be abandoned. (p-٣٣١) Or: what calls to it is a thing that he himself desires, and we do not know what it is, despite our cleverness. So it is a thing that is not known in itself.

When it was as if it were said, "What is the state of what he says?", they answered, adhering to imitation and the custom they had found their forefathers upon: ﴿We have not heard of this﴾, that is, of what you mention of monotheism, ﴿in the latter religion﴾. Their restricting it in this way indicates that they knew of it in the earlier religion, and that they recognized that Abraham (peace be upon him) and those of his descendants who were found, who were their fathers, down to 'Amr ibn Luhayy, were far from polytheism and constant in monotheism. Their only doubt was that He (glory be to Him) had not changed His dealings with them over these long periods. They also knew of resurrection, but they had forgotten it. Ibn al-Furat mentioned in his history the Day of Halima, one of the days of the Arabs, and said that Hajar ibn 'Amr, the one who ate the bitter plants (Akil al-Mirar), marched against the Banu Asad, killed them, and banished them to Tihama. 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said, among verses:

"You withheld Najd from them, so they settled in the mire of Tihama.
You are the king over them, and they are slaves until the Resurrection."

Imam Ahmad narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, the first to release the sawa'ib (free-roaming animals) and to worship idols was Abu Khuza'ah, 'Amr ibn 'Amir, and I saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire." Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first to change the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him) was 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qami'ah." Al-Bukhari, in "The Conquest of Mecca," narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that "the Prophet (ﷺ) removed from the House the image of Abraham and Isma'il (peace be upon them both), with the divining arrows in their hands, and said: 'May Allah fight them! They knew well that they never sought decisions by them.'" Thus what is said, that the people of the fatra (the interval between prophets) were ignorant with an ignorance that removed blame from them, is refuted. It is supported by what is in the Sahih from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, where is my father?' He said: 'In the Fire.' When the man turned away, he called him back and said: 'Indeed my father and your father are in the Fire.'" Muslim recorded it at the end of the Book of Faith. It has already passed in "Subhan," in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15], what benefits here. The decisive resolution of this dispute is His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, saying: Worship Allah and avoid the false deities. Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. This verse leaves no one until it encompasses him and judges him to Paradise or to the Fire.

Since the Prophet's (ﷺ) words alone were fit to shake them, how much more so when added to them was their knowledge that their forefathers, especially Isma'il and his father Abraham (peace be upon them both), held to it. They emphasized their statement with ﴿in﴾, that is, "what," ﴿this﴾, that is, what he says, ﴿is only a fabrication﴾, that is, deliberate lying. Yet there is no necessary connection between their not having heard of it and its being a fabrication; rather it is a saying whose meanings are known with slight reflection. Al-Tirmidhi, who said it is hasan sahih, and al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: "Abu Talib fell ill, so the Quraysh came to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came to him while there was a gathering of a man with Abu Talib. Abu Jahl stood up in order to prevent him." He said: "They complained about him to Abu Talib." Al-Nasa'i in al-Kabir and Abu Ya'la added: "And they said: 'He insults our gods.'" Abu Talib said: "O nephew, what do you want from your people?" He said: "I want from them one word, by which the Arabs will submit to them, and the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya (tax)." He said: "One word?!" He said: "One word." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah." They said: "Does he make the gods one god? We have not heard of this in the latter religion; this is only a fabrication." He said: "So the Qur'an was revealed about them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an containing the reminder﴾ [Sad: 1] ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2], up to His saying: ﴿fabrication﴾." It is mentioned in the exegetical works that they said: "How can one God encompass all creation?"

[p. 335] Since their purpose in these emphatic statements was to show that they were utterly firm in what they had been upon before his call, and since God refuses to let falsehood persist without a sign that exposes it and an authority that nullifies and tears it apart, He followed this with a report of their saying, which they took as evidence of his lying. This was a sign of the falsity of their assertion, which they stated with the utmost certainty, and it proclaimed that the root of their disease and what drove them to deny him was nothing but envy. He said, indicating by their expression "sent down" (inzal) that he was worthy of being suspected of prophethood because of the worship and noble conditions he had before the revelation, and they put first what indicates his particularity, out of obstinacy, because of what they knew of his circumstances that called for particularity, unlike what is mentioned concerning "al-Qamar." They also used the particle of elevation (ʿalā), indicating that one who says such a thing as he says could only be someone whose mind has been overwhelmed. So they said: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him?﴾, that is, to him alone, ﴿the Reminder﴾, that is, the one that contradicts what we are upon and by which he has come to be mentioned. They added explicitly what they had indicated by implication to show particularity, saying: ﴿from among us﴾, though we are older in years and greater in wealth. All of this, as you see, together with his proclaiming them to be possessed of great envy, proclaims them in the utmost way to be disgraced. For if the criterion were preserving the right of the forefathers, so that no one may change their religion or attack it with a newly invented religion, even if the proofs have been established for it and the evidences have converged to confirm its truth, then why did they change the religion of their forefathers on account of what ʿAmr ibn Luhayy introduced, a man who was not of their tribe, and bear witness against their forefathers to error, while they knew that what they had changed was the religion of Isma'il, and before him Ibrahim, and those who followed the two of them among the righteous among their descendants, peace be upon them? And if the criterion were the innovator, so that the changing of the religion of the prophets and those who followed them in goodness, peace be upon them, became permissible because of what ʿAmr ibn Luhayy introduced, then why do they not change what was introduced of error, by which the Prophet ﷺ came to them, and which they named "innovation"? And if the criterion were the truth, then why do they not examine the proofs and follow the arguments?

Since this indicated that they were not confident in what they had firmly asserted, He said: [p. 336] ﴿Rather﴾, that is, they are not certain of what they have said, however much they emphasized it, ﴿rather they are in doubt﴾, that is, in hesitation, encompassing them, beginning with them, ﴿concerning My Reminder﴾, that is, for this reason they do not remain firm upon one statement; that is, their states in their sayings and deeds are the states of one in doubt. He turned away from the manifestation of greatness to the singular, because this context is about tawhid, so the singular is more fitting for it, and in order that it be an explicit statement of the intended meaning after the mention of their gods, cutting off the doubts of their obstinate critics.

Since they were in reality certain of its truth, though their saying and doing was the saying of one in doubt, He said: ﴿Rather﴾, that is, they are not in doubt about it in reality, though their saying is the saying of one who is in doubt. And since they had experienced calamities and trials, hardships and tribulations, which perhaps led them to think that no punishment could be beyond them, He negated that they had tasted any of His punishment, which He sends when He wills vengeance. So He expressed it with what conveys the comprehensive negation over all of past time, and said: ﴿they have not yet tasted﴾, from the beginning of their affair until now, ﴿the punishment﴾, that is, which I have prepared for the deniers. So they are in arrogance and opposition; had they tasted it, the knots of their resolve would have been undone, and they would have become the most humiliated of things, the lowest, the most contemptible, and the least. And the consensus of the people of the rasm (the ʿUthmanic consonantal orthography of the Qur'an) and most of the readers on dropping its yāʾ in the script and in recitation indicates that this is the lesser punishment, which removes the zealotry of the jahiliyya (the age of ignorance). And Yaʿqub's alone affirming it in both states indicates that it is the punishment prepared for the destruction of the tyrannical nations, not punishment in general.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 9:

When their denial of his being singled out for the Remembrance (al-dhikr) — by negating their doubt, which necessarily implies affirmation that they know he is a messenger and that he is most worthy of the message — guided (the reader) to the sense of the implied meaning, namely: "Is there among them anyone other than him who is fit to receive this Remembrance, such that God should send it down upon him and leave aside this bringer of good tidings and warner ﷺ?" — He balanced with it His saying: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy﴾; that is, exclusively, to the exclusion of others; ﴿of your Lord﴾. Since sending down the revelation is a benefaction to the one upon whom it is sent down, He turned away from the singular pronoun to the attribute of benevolence, which conveys nurturing care; so He said — addressing him ﷺ, because it magnifies his station and exalts his rank and position — ﴿your Lord﴾; that is, the One who benefits you by sending it down; so that they might single out with it whomever they wish and withhold it from whomever they wish: ﴿Or do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32]. Since the one fit for lordship can only be the Victorious over everything other than Him, the One who bestows upon whomever He wills what He wills, He said: ﴿the Mighty, the Bestower﴾; that is, the One who overcomes every thing and is not overcome by anything, and who bestows, by way of grace, what He wills upon whom He desires; and He has the attribute of bestowing whose effects are continuous and perpetual (p-338). So there is no giver of what He withholds, nor any withholder of what He gives.

Since He had stripped them of authority over the treasuries, He followed this with the denial of sovereignty over what they had witnessed of them, which is a very small part. So He said: ﴿Or theirs is the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾; that is, exclusively; ﴿and what is between them﴾. Since the judgment regarding that does not necessarily entail judgment over the expanse (al-fada'), He said: ﴿and what is between them﴾; that is, so that their word would be the one executed in this existence, and they would speak about the divine matters and attribute whatever sublime affairs they wish to whomever they wish. Then He made their incapacity clear, rebuked them, reproached them, and censured them with what He stated as a consequence of that in His words: ﴿then let them ascend by the means﴾; that is, let them exert themselves to climb, if they have that ability; ﴿by the means﴾; that is, the paths leading to the heaven; so that they may sit upon the Throne, which is the sign of sovereignty, and thus govern the world and single out whomever they wish for prophethood. This is so that it may be known that they have such a right, and that it is not permissible for anyone to be singled out over them with anything.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 11:

When the characteristics of divinity had been negated from them (for what has passed) and from everyone they claim would back them or help them, such as their idols and others, this led to the conclusion that they are among His servants, glory be to Him. He therefore described their condition in the highest terms of their gathering and mutual support, which the preceding account had indicated: their arrogance, their defiance, their aversion to acceptance, and their unrestrained conduct. So He said, informing about a subject (mubtada', the implied subject) that was omitted because the knowledge of it is clear, (p-٣٣٩) ﴿a host of them﴾. That is: they are not among what has passed; rather, they are a host of contemptible people, from among our hosts, who help one another in supporting each other. Abu Hayyan said: It is also possible that "ma" is a descriptive particle, intended to convey either magnification by way of mockery of them, or belittlement, because the descriptive "ma" is used with both of these meanings. He also showed their distance from the position in which He had placed them and employed them, and from the ranks He had assigned to them, and their decline from those ranks, by His saying, describing "a host": ﴿there﴾. That is: in the lowest state, far from these lofty aims. He also showed that many of their like have banded together against the Messengers, but they harmed only themselves, by His saying, describing them after a description, singling them out for belittlement: ﴿routed﴾. That is: routing is a firmly established, constant attribute for them, ﴿of the confederates﴾. That is: those whose custom was arrogance and defiance, forming factions against the Prophets, and then the reversal of fortune falls upon them, while the final outcome belongs to the Messengers, peace be upon them. So do not be concerned with them at all. Ibn Burjan said: The first host routed among them was the host of the battle of Badr. Then the truth of this report spread (p-٣٤٠) to many hosts in various different battles.

When this (the verse's report of the Lord's decisive act of seizing those who denied) made people eager to learn about the earlier factions, and since they were the most insignificant of things in relation to Him, glorified is He, despite their strength in themselves, He explained this with the feminine marker (tā') indicating the second, later rank, which is the rank of the feminine, implying weakness. So He said: ﴿Denied﴾ (kadhdhabat). Since their intention was denial and nothing else, they were counted as covering all time, so the preposition was dropped and it was said: ﴿before them﴾, meaning, like their denial.

Since the first deniers had, in multitude, strength, unity, and endurance over long ages, what the later ones did not have, they were, despite being earliest in time, more deserving of being mentioned first in this context. So He said: ﴿the people of Noah﴾. They persisted in their arrogance and opposition until they saw the water had seized them, and they did not allow themselves to submit, nor to humble themselves before Noah, peace be upon him, asking to board with him or that he pray for them so they might be saved.

Since the people of Hud, peace be upon him, after them had a grandeur and might that others lacked, along with the strength of their bodies, the loftiness of their aspirations, and the vastness of their dominion, to the point that they built a garden on earth, He followed them with them. Their connection to them lies in the fact that their punishment was by the wind, which is the cause of the clouds carrying water. So He said: ﴿And ʿĀd﴾, naming them by the name that alerts to the power they had through sovereignty. They also persisted in their opposition until the wind came out upon them, and they saw it carrying camels between heaven and earth, and its first gusts overtook them, while they saw Hud, peace be upon him, and those with him of the believers, may Allah be pleased with them, in safety from it. Their opposition did not let them ask him to pray for them, nor did they submit to what he called them to.

Since they had, in strength and dominion over the whole earth, and in the building of Iram of the pillars, what made the dominion of every king appear small beside it, He followed them with a mighty ruler who overpowered others by the might of his authority and the multitude of his helpers, until he claimed divinity in his time, and magnified himself with the vastness of his dominion and the rivers flowing beneath him. Along with this, there is his agreement with them in that his punishment was by wind, inwardly, though it was by water, outwardly. This is because when Moses, peace be upon him, struck the sea, Allah sent the wind, which divided it into paths and dried those paths. When the Children of Israel had passed safely through, Allah (exalted be He) commanded the wind and it became still, so the sea closed over Pharaoh and his people. So He (exalted be He) said: ﴿And Pharaoh﴾, naming him explicitly to establish the reality of his affair and to state plainly his disbelief, nullifying what the wicked had displayed of baseness, slandering the religion, and casting doubt upon the weak among the Muslims.

When He explicitly stated his disbelief, He described him with what indicates, along with indicating that he shared with ʿĀd in the magnitude of the matter, the disbelief of his people. So He said: ﴿the possessor of stakes﴾ (dhū al-awtād), meaning the causes that make dominion firm and strengthen it: the elevation of authority through the multitude of helpers, the singularity of commands, breadth of intellect, subtlety of scheming, abundance of stratagems through sorcery and other means, excellence of management through justice (so he claimed), and the force of dominance. Abu Hayyan said: its origin is from the tent secured by its stakes. al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"The tent is not built except with a pillar,
and there is no support if its stakes are not driven."

They persisted in arrogance and opposition, being struck sometimes by the flood, sometimes by locusts, sometimes by lice, another time by frogs, and by other things, until they saw the sign of the sea, which was the final end. None of that turned them back from their opposition, until they drowned in their disbelief, every last one of them, as this verse declares explicitly.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 13:

When Thamud were the greatest of people after them in what they had of skilled construction in the mountains and plains, and in their expansiveness in cultivating gardens, channeling springs, and other matters, along with their resemblance to them in seeing great, manifest, perceptible signs, He followed them with them, saying: ﴿And Thamud﴾. They persisted in what they were engaged in until they saw the signs of punishment: yellowness of faces, then redness, then blackness. Nothing restrained them from their arrogance and opposition.

When the one that drove Thamud to the sin that necessitated punishment was women—since the one who hamstrung the she-camel did not dare to hamstring her except for a woman among them, who made her bridal portion conditional upon his hamstringing her—and the one that necessitated the punishment of the people of Lot was the mounting of males, the thing that unites them is lust for the private parts, together with the antithesis of males and females. Yet the punishment of Thamud was by the quaking of their abodes, and the punishment of the people of Lot was by uprooting their cities, lifting them and then overturning them. He followed them with them, saying—expressing by what indicates their strength, and attributing them to their prophet, peace be upon him, because they were a number of cities with no single comprehensive name, like the people of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿and the people of Lot﴾; that is, those who had the power to carry out what they attempted. They persisted in their arrogance and opposition until they were struck with blindness and their eyes were obliterated, and they were unable to reach what they intended of entering the house of Lot, peace be upon him, nor to achieve what they wanted. That did not turn them back from their arrogance and opposition; rather, they threatened him with the rising of the day.

When He mentioned the people of the settled areas (ahl al-madar), He followed them with a group from the people of the tents (ahl al-wabar), who approach them in disobedience through the trees, along with the fact that their punishment was by a cloud of fire, just as the people of Lot, peace be upon him, had stones of fire. So He said: ﴿And the companions of the thicket﴾. Then He magnified their matter, to belittle the matter of Quraysh and to deter them, by urging the recollection of their punishment. So He said: ﴿Those are the factions﴾; that is, the great ones in mustering troops and gathering against those who oppose them, ﴿the factions﴾; that is, those whose highest rank in opposition is to be like one faction of them.

(p-٣٤٤) When the context was one of opposition, of their gathering against him, their unity in hostility, which is falsehood, and their agreement, and since they, because of the obstinacy they held and the zealotry of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance), would at times deny that the destruction of these factions was on account of their denial, and would say: "It is the custom of time to destroy, and of differing in the causes of destruction," He said, emphasising with various kinds of emphasis: ﴿Not﴾, that is, "mā"; ﴿each one﴾ of these groups had a cause for its destruction among the causes; ﴿except﴾ that it ﴿denied the messengers﴾, that is, all of them, by denying His messenger. For whoever denies one messenger, while his prophethood is established, has belittled the one who sent him, and this necessarily entails denying all whom He sends, because the proofs (mu'jizat) through which their prophethood was established are equal in obliging belief. ﴿So My retribution was due﴾, that is, as a consequence of that denial, it was certain that ﴿retribution﴾ was due, that is, it was established against him, so that he could not escape it in any way. The shift to the singular pronoun together with the first-person style is because the context is one of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), as has passed, and it is more explicit regarding the intended meaning. The secret of omitting the yā' in writing in all the copies of the Qur'an (mashāḥif), and in recitation according to most of the reciters (qurrā'), and of affirming it in both states for Ya'qub alone, has been mentioned before.

Since the context is one of dissension, and of submitting to the Reminder, which is the admonition of honour:

؎ The lofty noble does not escape harm,
 until blood is spilled on its sides.

the situation required punishment, unlike what is in Surah Qaf, for the context there concerns their denial of resurrection, (p-٣٤٥) the validity of warning, and the affirmation of glory, so the threat there sufficed.

Since the sense requires a ﴿و﴾ ... "wa" linking clause, the intended construction is: "Indeed We had repaid each of those factions [with punishment] when the punishment was due against them, with a kind of retribution about which no one has any doubt or uncertainty." Then he joined to it his saying: ﴿And not﴾. Since the Quraysh were in extreme obstinacy, insistence on disbelief, arrogance against submitting to the truth, and pursuit of every cause of punishment, it was as though they were awaiting it and seeking to hasten it, so he expressed it with what indicates waiting. Since they, by their knowledge of the truthfulness of what was coming to them and their certainty in the soundness of what he said, were as though they were seeing the punishment and not turning back, he stripped the verb of waiting and said: ﴿they await﴾ (yanzuru). He belittled them with his saying: ﴿these﴾, meaning: those who have turned away from you in pride and opposition, whose utmost effort is to be among the factions who banded together against Our soldiers. So We seized them with what is well known of Our battles and familiar from Our days, with various kinds of punishment. Their multitude did not avail them anything, nor did their strength, and their weakness or fewness did not harm Our soldiers: ﴿except a single cry﴾. He belittled their affair by indicating that the least of His punishment suffices to destroy them, so he said ﴿single﴾ (wahidah). Since the context is one of threat, it is known from this that the description with oneness is for magnification. He clarified this with his saying: ﴿there is none for it﴾, meaning, for the cry, ﴿any respite﴾ (fawaq), meaning any increase of anything of its kind that would be above it. It is said: "faqa asḥabahu fawqan wa fawaqan," meaning he rose above them. Hamzah read it with a ḍammah (fuwaq), so it becomes a metaphor for the speed of destruction by it, without any delay at all, since al-fuwaq, like ghurab (on the pattern of a noun), is what seizes the dying person at the moment of death throes. The meaning is that in destroying them He needs nothing beyond the described cry, since there is no cry above it. In this there is magnification of the least of His punishment and belittling of the highest of their affair. It is also permissible that the two readings derive from "fawaq al-ḥalb" (the interval of milking). Al-Saghani said: "al-fuwaq" and "al-fawaq" (that is, with ḍammah and with fatḥah) are the time between the two milkings, because it is milked and then left briefly so that the young camel may suckle it to let the milk down again. In al-Qamus he said: or the interval between opening your hand and closing it on the udder. So the meaning is: there is no return for it, as milk returns into the udder after the interval, and as the sick person returns to health by recovering from illness. Or the meaning is: there is no separation or interruption for it, to the extent that anyone could take a breath, however small and however brief in time, as is the custom of familiar sounds, in which there is a echoing that causes the sound to break up, so that its impact becomes weak and dull, and its emission loose. Rather, it is a deafening sound, of one pattern, which startles no one without killing him, except whom Allah (Exalted) makes firm. It is also permissible that it derives from the fawaq of the dying person, meaning that there is nothing in it preceding death except the striking of the sound. This agrees with their saying: "there is no reprieve or rest for it." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 16:

When He had marveled at them for what had passed, and had nullified their doubts, and made them aware that they had exposed themselves to destruction in a near exposure, He followed that with a marvel greater than the first. So He said: ﴿And they said﴾; that is, mockingly, not fearing what We had threatened them with, nor considering its outcome: ﴿Our Lord﴾; that is, O You who are good to us; ﴿hasten for us﴾; that is, as a kindness to us, ﴿our qitt﴾; that is, our share of the punishment with which we have been threatened, and our record in which You wrote that and in which You counted our deeds. Its origin is from "qadda al-shay'" (he cut the thing), if he cut it; and from it "qadda al-qalam" (he cut the pen); and its most common usage is in writing.

Since the intent of this was exaggeration in mockery, by asking for punishment at all times between them and the Resurrection, they dropped the preposition and said: ﴿before the Day of Reckoning﴾; so they made the whole time between them and it a time-frame for that. They made its hastening a kindness toward them, as a sign of extreme mockery. He expressed it with qitt to add emphasis to the warning about following desire without evidence, for its root is mostly concerned with what is disliked. Its derivation is from "al-qatt," which is cutting. So "al-qitt" means: a share; a written document; and a book of reckoning, because it is a piece of paper; and reckoning is a piece of affairs, in which one decides what belongs to him; and the Hour, because it is a piece of time. "Taqaqqata al-rajul" means: he rode his head, i.e., followed his desire, which is a piece of his affair. "Ja'at al-khayl qataqita" means: horses came in pieces, i.e., pieces and groups, in scattering. "Al-qatt" means cutting; "al-qatat" means short and curly-haired; and "al-taqtaqa" means imitating the sound of stones. So it is as if they said: hasten for us of that what is certain, with no doubt about it, and whose sound is heard at the utmost intensity, so it destroys, separates loved ones, is written in every document, and its report is recited through all the ages. For that is that We do not turn back from it for anything at all. So glory be to the Forbearing, who honored us and showed mercy to us through the Prophet of mercy, so He did not hasten vengeance upon us, and turned our hearts toward him, and restricted our aspirations to him, after they had been in the greatest distance.

When the flood had reached the crests of the hills in their persistence in falsehood out of obstinacy, and its overflow had surpassed the peaks of the heights, and their request for the punishment to be hastened was mockery, along with what they had already put forward of denial and far-from-right speech, it might have called for the request to hasten what they sought. It might also have led to the assumption that their aversion and the trial they inflicted were due to something in the message or in the one who conveyed it. (Allah, exalted is He) made clear that His custom is to test the righteous, to raise their ranks. So He said, (exalted is He), consoling, comforting, and giving solace to this noble Prophet (ﷺ) by means of the prophets and messengers who preceded him among his brothers (p-349), reminding him of the hardships they endured and the trials they faced, urging him to act in their manner, commanding him to patience, deliberation, and forbearance, and warning him against haste, impatience, and weariness. He began with the people of nobility, because the context concerns the nobility of the Qur'an, which entails the nobility of its bearer. This is to make known that nobility does not necessarily entail ease in this world, and to alert that his nobility will soon require him, because of the abundance of followers, to judge between those with disputes and conflicts, a task which has no stability except through forbearance, deliberation, and patience. He began with those of nobility with one whose early situation was like the early situation of this noble Prophet (ﷺ), in that his people oppressed him, and whose final situation was a king of firm foundations and awe-inspiring authority, so that his condition would serve as an example for him and complete consolation would be achieved through it. (Allah said): ﴿Be patient﴾ over what they say. He indicated by the particle of elevation the great degree of patience, saying: ﴿over what﴾, and he increased the exhortation to it by using the present tense, saying: ﴿they say﴾, meaning they renew their saying at every moment of the harmful, painful, and tearful words. For indeed it is not due to any deficiency in you, but for wisdoms too great to describe, the foundation of which is the increase of your nobility and the elevation of your ranks. He turned the speech toward the station of majesty, because what is mentioned of subjugation requires it: ﴿And remember Our servant﴾, meaning the one whom We purified for Ourselves and who purified himself to look upon Our greatness and to stand in Our service. He substituted for it, or clarified it, with His saying: ﴿David, the possessor of strength﴾, meaning the great powers in freeing his soul from the attachments of bodies, so his strength in that was a cause for his ascent to the great ranks.

Since the greatest struggle is rescuing oneself from the pits of lapses and the commands of desires, by ascending the stairways of perfections and the ladders of turning toward Allah, and since that is hardly found among human beings, because they are surrounded by desires and have been given heedlessness in their natures, He gave the reason for his strength by saying, emphatically: ﴿Indeed, he was oft-returning﴾, meaning returning often to Allah (exalted is He), so that he would return to that upon which He created him, in the best of forms, by pure reason. He applied "elevation" degree by degree to the return, because that is below the rank that becomes the final end at death. It is as if the one decreed for it had lowered himself from it, then began returning to it at every moment, through what he endured of struggles, confrontations, and attempts, until he reached it after being stripped of all desire.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 18:

Since a person continually draws near to God (exalted is He) until He loves him, and once He loves him He acts toward him (glory be to Him), and extraordinary events (khawariq, miracles that break habitual patterns) appear through his hands, He said, beginning a new sentence (musta'nifan), as an answer to one who asked about His reward for that struggle (jihad), emphasizing it (muakkidan lahu) because humanity is naturally disposed to deny extraordinary events, being confined to what is familiar (al-ma'lufat): ﴿Indeed We﴾, that is, with the greatness We possess, which nothing can overpower; ﴿subjected the mountains﴾, that is, those which are harder than the hearts of your people, for they are the hardest of lands, most firm, most lofty, and most exalted, by making them submissive and tractable like a docile camel. He then restricted this by His saying ﴿along with him﴾, that is, accompanying him; so this subjection was not manifested to anyone before him or after him. And since the mountains' glorifying (tasbih) came gradually, which was more wondrous because they are inanimate, He used the present tense (fi'l mudari'), saying, depicting that state and expressing it with the feminine pronoun, indicating that after their hardness they became extremely soft and yielding: ﴿they glorified﴾ (yusabbihna), with each mountain glorifying in a voice not resembling the voice of another, because that is closer to distinction and to knowing each one's glorification individually. He did not say "musabbihah" or "tusabbihu," lest it be thought that their glorification was in a single voice, which would make the matter unclear regarding some of them. It is possible that this is a new sentence, and possible that it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning that they submit to Him in glorification, by speech and by state, like the submission of one who freely and obediently obeys God.

Since the context concerns returning (al-awba), and since the end of the day is the time when everyone with a habitual place returns to it, and although it is also the time of lassitude and rest from fatigue, He said: ﴿in the evening﴾ (al-'ashiyy), that is, to strengthen the one who acts and to remind the heedless. And since the context concerns overflowing grace and honoring with the Qur'an, He said: ﴿and at sunrise﴾ (al-ishraq), that is, at the time when the sun has risen above the time when people are scattered in their occupations and preoccupied with food and pleasures, in words and deeds, as a reminder to them and a turning back from their habits toward sanctifying their Lord (glory be to Him). Ishraq is not the sunrise itself; rather, it is the sun's clarity and brightness, and shuruq is its rising. Umm Hani' (may God be pleased with her) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the duha (forenoon prayer) in her house and said to her: "This is the prayer of ishraq." In al-Jami' of Abd al-Razzaq, it is related that Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: "The duha prayer is in the Qur'an, but only one who dives deep will reach it," and then he recited this verse. The reference here is also, God knows best, to the prayer of the awwabin (those who turn back repeatedly to God): ﴿Remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed he was ever turning back (awwab)﴾ [Sad: 17] ﴿And We gave Dawud Sulayman; an excellent servant; indeed he was ever turning back﴾ [Sad: 30] ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba: 10] ﴿And the birds gathered; each was to him one who turns back﴾ [Sad: 19]. Muslim in his Sahih, Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad, and al-Darimi in his Jami' known as al-Musnad, narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam (may God be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The prayer of the awwabin is when the young camels are scorched." The wording of al-Darimi is: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to them while they were praying after sunrise, and said: 'The prayer of the awwabin is when the young camels are scorched.'" The wording of Abd is: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to them in the mosque of Quba and saw them praying the duha, and said: 'This is the prayer of the awwabin.' They used to pray it when the young camels were scorched." That is, when they kneel down from the intensity of the heat and its burning of their hooves, from "ramas" (with a vowel on the middle letter), which is the intensity of the sun on sand and other things; and "ramda'" means very hot.

(p-353) When Allah, glorified is He, informed of the subjugation of the heaviest and most firmly fixed of things to Him, He followed it with the lightest and most mobile of them. He expressed them by a noun that denotes collectivity as a whole and steadiness, because it is more indicative of power. So He said, using the collective noun rather than the plural, to indicate that they are in a state of extreme gathering, as if they were one single thing; He described their state with an attribute suited to the singular, and made it feminine, to indicate the softness that is inherent in females, which entails utmost compliance and acceptance of the disposition of rulings. ﴿And the birds﴾; that is, We subjugated them to him, in a state of being ﴿gathered﴾; that is, brought together to him, compelled, from every direction, all at once (what the use of the noun rather than the verb indicates), and this is more indicative of power, for they are more prone to flight and harder to control. This is like the pebbles that glorified Allah in the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in the hand of some of his Companions; and like the mountain that shook, and he struck it with his foot and said: "Be still, Uhud, for upon you are a Prophet, a truthful man, and two martyrs," so it was still; and like the hornets that gathered upon the head of 'Asim ibn Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah, may Allah be pleased with him, and prevented anyone from taking his body so that it would not be disgraced, and when night came Allah sent a torrent that carried him away to a place where no news of him was known and no trace of him was found. ﴿Each﴾; that is, each one of the mountains and the birds; ﴿turned in repentance to Him﴾; that is, returned frequently; in order to (for the sake of) Dawud, peace be upon him, specifically (p-354) away from its habitual course, not in any other sense from what they were accustomed to. So whenever he turned back from his judgment, and from what he was engaged in of occupation with creation, to glorifying the Truth, they too returned with him in that, the mountains and the birds. The report was given in the singular to indicate the intensity of their chanting with the discipline and the magnitude of him; and the singular also conveys a ruling upon each individual, whereas had it been in the plural it would admit the possibility that the ruling applies to the group as a collective under the condition of plurality. So it is as if Dawud, peace be upon him, understood the glorification of the mountains and the birds, and each of them submitted to him whenever he commanded them to glorify; and everyone who is truly realized in his state is aided by everything, as al-Qushayri said. In this there is an indication to the Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever We wish, We make your people with you in subjugation in this manner; so do not despair of them despite the intensity of their aversion, and the strength of their foolishness and delusion, for We have made them so that you may train yourself through them, and increase in majesty, exaltedness, elevation and perfection through patience with them, along with other wisdoms that minds cannot encompass. And do not despair of their softening toward you and their returning to you, for they are no more than mountains in strength and firmness, or birds in aversion, levity and lightness; so whenever We wish, We make them for you like what We made the mountains and birds with Dawud, peace be upon him; rather, their affair is easier and their condition more lenient.

When this was indicative of sovereignty, in that it is the exercise of authority over great matters by force, it was as if it were said: all of that is to affirm his prophethood and to magnify his kingship. (p-355) He said: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾; i.e., by what We possess of greatness; ﴿his kingdom﴾, without other than that which a king needs. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he was the most powerful of the kings of the earth in authority.

And since the greatest of the things that establish kingship is knowledge, He said: ﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾; i.e., by Our greatness; ﴿wisdom﴾; i.e., prophethood, from which arises knowledge of things as they are, and the placing of things in their most fitting places. Thus wisdom is acting upon knowledge. And since its completion is by ending dispute, He said: ﴿and decisive speech﴾; i.e., and knowing the distinguishing point between what is ambiguous in the speech of those who address him, without great deliberation in that; rather he distinguishes intuitively between the similar matters, such that he leaves no confusion through which a dispute could arise with an obstinate opponent. And We clothed him with honor, awe, and dignity that prevents anyone from daring to be obstinate about any matter of his after that clarification, which separated the similar matters and distinguished the obscure difficulties. And when he speaks, he stops at the joints, so from his unfolding of the discourse he makes its meanings clear, and places each thing in its most sound foundations.

(p. 356) Since the context is training in patience, firm and healing steadfastness, complete reflection, and the trial of those close to God, and since one who has been given decisive speech (﴿fasl al-khitab﴾, "decisive speech") is expected not to be confused about a judgment or hasty in a matter, and since the implied question was, "Has this news come to you?", he connected it to what precedes it, explaining the consequences of haste. He informs us that whoever has been given knowledge should always look to the One who gave him that knowledge, asking Him for understanding and seeking to be made capable (*istij'az*, seeking to be enabled) for himself, while picturing the station of servanthood (*ubudiyyah*). This station is emphasized repeatedly in this surah, as in His saying, "Excellent is the servant." He says, in a context whose outward form is a question and whose inner meaning is a warning about the strangeness and wonder in it, so that the desire to hear it becomes great and it is retained with full attention: ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ That is, its news is very great. He used the singular, although the intended meaning is plural, to indicate that they were of one word in displaying the enmity, so that none of them appeared to be an intermediary, and similar things.

Since *al-khasm* (the adversary/disputant) is a verbal noun that applies to one or more, male or female, and since it is permissible to call a group of disputants "an adversary" because they are in the form of an adversary, He said: ﴿when they climbed over﴾, that is, the news of their dispute when they ﴿climbed over﴾, meaning they ascended the wall, and they and those with them descended from it, derived from *al-sawr*, which is leaping over. ﴿the prayer niche (al-mihrab)﴾, that is, the most noble part of the place of worship, in which Dawud, peace be upon him, used to be. This is a metaphor for their having come to him on a day of worship and not through the door, thereby contravening the custom of people in both respects. It seems that the prayer niche they climbed into had a door inside another door.

(p-357) He drew attention to this by making ﴿إذ﴾ (idh, "when") a substitute (badal) for the first "idh" (idh, "when"), that is, the time "when they entered" (﴿دخلوا﴾). He named him explicitly, to remove any ambiguity and to indicate his nearness in rank and his great affection, saying: ﴿upon Dawud﴾, as a trial from Us for him, together with his great sovereignty and his high nearness to Us. He showed that this occurred in a manner that alarmed him, either because he was in a place where no one could reach him or for some other reason, by saying: ﴿so he was startled﴾, that is, he was frightened, alarmed and afraid ﴿of them﴾, that is, despite his great sovereignty, his courage of heart, his knowledge of wisdom and the might of his authority.

Since it was as if it were said, "What did they say to him?", he said: ﴿They said, "Do not fear.">. Since this would cause his thoughts about their matter to wander in every direction, they specified their situation by saying: ﴿"Two disputants"﴾, that is, we are two parties in a dispute. Then they explained this by saying: ﴿"One of us has wronged the other"﴾, that is, he sought to rise above and dominate, ﴿"over the other"﴾. They first left it vague so that they could then give the details, which would have a stronger effect on the soul. Since his asking about the judgment followed from this, they said: ﴿"So judge between us with truth"﴾, that is, with the matter that is established and that reality corresponds to. They asked him this even though they knew he would judge only with justice, so that he would be the more deserving of rebuke at the slightest lapse. ﴿"And do not deviate"﴾, that is, do not cause distance or go beyond the limit, neither in the expression of that, such that our meaning becomes unclear to us, nor in anything else. (p-358) Or: do not go to excess in pursuing the subtle details of matters, for I am content with the truth in its simplest forms. For this reason it was expressed with the quadriliteral (rubā'ī) form, and with the triliteral (thulāthī) form in the same meaning. Abu 'Ubayd said: "shatta fi al-hukm" and "ashatta", when he acted unjustly. For this reason too he left the idgham (assimilation of the doubled letters) unassimilated, as an indication that the prohibition is only against an extremely clear deviation. Since the truth has a highest, a lowest and a middle, they asked to be guided to the middle, so they said: ﴿"And guide us"﴾, that is, direct us, ﴿"to the even"﴾, that is, the middle ﴿"of the path"﴾, that is, the clear way, so that there is no inclination toward either side by means of the middle course: neither excess in pursuing the fine points of the matter, nor negligence in neglecting them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 23:

Since this claim concerns a matter so strange that almost no one hears it without denying it, he framed the speech with emphasis, saying: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, pointing to a person among those who entered. Then he put in apposition to it his saying: ﴿my brother﴾, meaning in religion and companionship. Then he informed about him with his saying: ﴿has ninety-nine ewes﴾. It is also permissible that "my brother" is the predicate, and the emphasis in that case is for the sake of making the quarrel of a brother, and his aggression against his brother, seem unlikely. What follows would then be a resumptive statement: ﴿and I have one ewe﴾, meaning: I, O claimant. ﴿A single ewe﴾: since that could be understood as a collective noun, he emphasized it with his saying: ﴿one﴾. Then he made his saying ﴿so he said﴾ follow from it, meaning: the one who has the majority. ﴿Entrust her to me﴾, meaning: give her to me, so that I may be her guardian. ﴿And he overpowered me﴾, meaning: he defeated me, prevailed over me, grew strong, and dealt harshly with me ﴿in speech﴾, meaning: in the kind of talk that carries weight, such as argument and other things (p-359), by arguing with me until he wearied me, so I fell silent, unable to continue contending with him, and he would not be satisfied from me with anything short of his aim.

When the claim was complete, the desire for an answer arose, so His saying ﴿He said﴾ was introduced anew; that is, on the assumption that what you have said is correct. This is because when he saw that the opponent had fallen silent and had not denied anything of what the claimant said, and perhaps had shown a bearing indicating his assent, he said that, and was rebuked, even though there was an excuse for him. All of this was to train him to be careful in judgment, not to lean toward circumstantial evidence, and not to be content in it except with something like the sun. He emphasized his statement in the form of an oath, as a deterrent to the wrongdoer, on the assumption that the claim is correct, by exaggerating in denying his act, because the state of one who does something indicates a denial that he is a wrongdoer and that his act is an injustice. He opened his statement with the particle of anticipation (ḥarf al-tawaqquʿ), because the circumstance of the claim requires it: ﴿Indeed he has wronged you﴾; that is, by God, he has placed what he did with you in other than its proper place, on the assumption that your claim is correct; ﴿by demanding your ewe﴾; that is, by asking you to add it; and he indicated that this was in the manner of exclusiveness by his saying ﴿to his ewes﴾, whether by himself or by another acting on his behalf; for this reason he did not say "by demanding his." Then he joined to that a general matter comprising them and others, as an admonition, an encouragement, and a warning. Since mixing (khulṭah) necessarily gives rise to the presumption of familiarity, because of the presence of justice and equity, and the improbability of oppression existing alongside it, he emphasized his statement, admonishing the transgressor if there was one, and hinting at forbearance and reconciliation for the wronged party: ﴿Indeed, many of the associates [khulaṭāʾ] wrong one another﴾; that is, in general, from among you and from among others; ﴿so that some of them oppress [yabghī] others﴾; that is, they overstep and act arrogantly, seeking what is not right; ﴿except those who believe﴾ among the associates; ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾; that is, in confirmation of their claimed faith; ﴿the righteous deeds﴾; that is, all of them; for such people do not commit oppression. ﴿And few are they﴾; he emphasized their scarcity and expressed wonder at it by the indefinite in his saying ﴿mā﴾, like "how excellent" (niʿimmā), and "for some matter" (wa-li-amrin mā); ﴿they﴾; and he postponed this subject and placed the predicate first, out of concern for it, because the purpose is to express intense regret that justice is in extremely short supply; that is, so take them as a model, O claimant, and be among them, O defendant.

When that was complete, the two who had entered upon him departed, and he saw none of them. It occurred to him that there was no dispute, and that they had only intended to test him in judgment and train him in it; and that it is permissible for a person to say what has not occurred if a great benefit is built upon it, which facilitates that speech as a means to reaching it, or was the best of the ways, while the matter is free of corruption. Its essence is that he recalled a statement, and what is meant by it is some of its necessary implications; it is like the indication of the inclusive meaning (dalālat al-tadammun) in single words. This is like the saying of Solomon, peace be upon him: "Bring me a knife, that I may split it between them," and his intention was nothing but what follows from that of recognizing the truthful and the liar, by the mother's refusal of it and the other claimant's acceptance of falsehood. And the verification of this is that there is no necessary connection between speech and the intending of a meaning that corresponds exactly to the words' individual terms, as evidenced by the idle oath (laghw al-yamīn), and by the Prophet ﷺ saying to Ṣafiyyah, may God be pleased with her, "ʿAqrā ḥalqā" [may you be barren, may you be bald], and to Umm Salamah, may God be pleased with her, "Tariba yamīnuki" [may your right hand be dust-covered]; and his saying ﷺ: "Three things are serious in their seriousness and their jesting is also serious," indicates that speech may not be intended in its literal meaning. From here arose the ruling regarding words of allusion (kināyāt) that nothing takes effect by them unless it is accompanied by the intention of the meaning. And since this amount was known, he followed it with His saying ﴿And David thought﴾; that is, that they had left before the matter was decided; and a great matter from the greatness of God had befallen him, the like of which he had never experienced; ﴿that We had tested him﴾; that is, We had examined him by this judgment in matters of the kind that kings must face, so that their condition might become clear in them; and he knew that he had hastened to attribute to the defendant that he had wronged, before hearing his words and before the claimant asked him for judgment; so God rebuked him for that, and the prophets, peace be upon them, because of the elevation of their stations, are rebuked for the like of this. It is of the nature of restricting the attribute to the qualified (qaṣr al-mawṣūf ʿalā al-ṣifah) in reverse; that is, this story is restricted to the trial, and has no connection with the dispute. Had the intended meaning been what is said about the story of the woman, which every Muslim is obliged to exonerate, along with the rest of his brothers, peace be upon them, from the like of it, it would have been said "And David knew," and not "And David thought" — as every person with even slight taste in discourse bears witness. And God is the Granter of success. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and al-Ḥārith al-Aʿwar that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, said: "Whoever tells you the story of David as the storytellers narrate it, I will flog him a hundred and sixty times," and that is the prescribed penalty for slander against the prophets, peace be upon them. It is also reported that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was told this story while a man of the people of truth was with him, and he denied what the narrator had said and stated: "If the story is as it is in the Book of God, mighty and majestic, then it is not proper to seek anything contrary to it; and how great it is to say otherwise! And if it is as you have mentioned, and God withheld it as a veil over His Prophet ﷺ, then it is not proper to make it manifest to him." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "My hearing this statement is dearer to me than all that the sun has risen upon."

That story and its like are from the lies of the Jews; and some of those who embraced Islam from among them informed me that they deliberately do this concerning David, peace be upon him, because Jesus, peace be upon him, is of his progeny, so that they might find a way to slander him.

When he thought this, He caused him to realize what God described of his returning; so He expressed that by His saying ﴿and he sought forgiveness﴾; and when the greatness that is the destination of this overwhelmed him, he returned to mention kindness and gentleness, and said ﴿his Lord﴾; that is, he sought forgiveness from his master, who had done him good by placing him in that great station, from returning to the first judgment without hearing the other; ﴿and fell down﴾; that is, he dropped from his standing, repenting to his Lord from that; and since falling down may be for other than worship, He said ﴿bowing [rākiʿan]﴾; that is, prostrating; because falling down is only for falling to the ground; and because the Prophet ﷺ explained it as prostration, as narrated by al-Nasāʾī from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "The Prophet ﷺ prostrated in Ṣād and said: 'David prostrated for it in repentance, and we prostrate for it in thankfulness.'" He expressed prostration by bowing (rukūʿ) so that it would be understood that he did it from standing, and that he was extremely swift, because of the intensity of his concern with it and the abundance of the motive for it, to the extent that he reached prostration in the time it takes others to reach bowing. Ibn al-Tayyānī said in his book "al-Mūʿib": "Everything that falls onto its face, so that its knee touches the ground after lowering its head, is rākiʿ." Ibn Durayd said: "The rākiʿ is one who falls on his face." End of quotation. And "al-rukʿah," with a damma, is a pit in the ground, as if it was named so because one falls into it on the face; and as if it were the root of the word. And in the Qāmūs: "rakaʿa," meaning he prayed; so then the meaning becomes: he fell praying; and it is known that their prayer had no bowing in it; and this was mentioned earlier in Āl ʿImrān and al-Baqarah. ﴿And turned in repentance [anāba]﴾; that is, he repented; meaning he returned from returning to the like of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 25:

Since the situation could be ambiguous in reporting the forgiveness if he had used the third-person pronoun, for it would give the impression that his Lord was other than the One speaking, and since forgiveness is only fitting together with power, he returned to the manifestation of greatness, affirming perfection and negating deficiency. So He said: ﴿So We forgave him﴾; that is: because of that, and following it, with Our greatness and the completeness of Our power, a forgiveness whose magnitude befits what We possess of greatness. ﴿And he had that﴾; that is: the falling into speaking about attributing wrongdoing to someone without hearing his speech. The Prophet ﷺ had stipulated with his Lord, glorified is He, for the sake of this story, that whoever reviled him or invoked a curse upon him, while not being deserving of it, it would be for that person a blessing, mercy and prayer. The summary is that this incident was for training the Prophet ﷺ in patience toward his people. Second, this sura, according to what was narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd, is among the earliest revealed in Makkah. This is also indicated by the earlier hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning the complaint of the polytheists about him ﷺ to his uncle Abu Talib, that he spoke against their gods; for that was at the beginning of the affair, since when the Prophet ﷺ first called them he was not commanded to mention their gods, so they did not answer him, and they did not withdraw from him entirely. Then Allah commanded him to mention their gods, and then they opposed him at that time (p-365) and kept away from him, and they preceded this with complaints to Abu Talib, time after time, so that he would restrain him from it. So this claim was a training for Dawud, peace be upon him, in judgments; and mentioning it to the Prophet ﷺ was a training for him in deliberation in all his affairs at all times.

Since mentioning this may have given the impression of something regarding the Prophet's ﷺ station, there was brought in an emphatic style His saying: ﴿And indeed for him﴾; that is: along with the forgiveness and the greatness of that, by the manifestation of greatness; because what is attributed to the Great is never anything but great. So He said: ﴿with Us﴾; and He increased in showing concern with that, negating what may have been suspected; so He emphasized His saying: ﴿a station of nearness﴾; that is: a great nearness, established after forgiveness; ﴿and a good place of return﴾; that is: a destination, in everything that is hoped for of good; and beyond that. So this is instructive, and there is no doubt that this affair was not brought up except for the elevation in ranks of perfection, and nothing else. The most evident proof of what I have mentioned is that this trial was only in training in judgment, not because of a woman or anything else; and that what they mentioned of the story of the woman is false, even if it is widespread; for how many a widely known and mentioned falsehood is the very essence of falsehood. His saying (Exalted is He) after it, in the form of drawing a lesson from it, turning speech away from the manifestation of greatness toward direct address with sweet discourse, in the manner of what passes between beloveds:

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 26:**

﴿O Dawud!﴾ Since the content of the report is meant to increase its grandeur, and it is of a kind that human souls may find hard to accept, He emphasized it for this reason. He also made it explicit, because it is something to be desired for its goodness and its beautiful effect, and it energizes the one who mentions it to the utmost degree of activity. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We﴾, that is, with the greatness that belongs to Us, ﴿have made you﴾, so do not reckon any of its causes as a calculation, and do not fear any consequence from it, ﴿a khalifa (vicegerent)﴾, that is, on Our behalf, executing Our commands among Our servants. So your judgment is Our judgment. He omitted what is known to be intended, such as "We said," to indicate that he was addressed with these delightful words when he had finished prostrating, as a notification of the truth of his expectation. He said: ﴿on the earth﴾, that is, all of it, indicating that his authority is unrestricted over all of it, so there is no blame on him for what he does in any land he wishes. He did not mention what was made a khalifa over, in order to magnify him, by pointing out that everything the intellect permits concerning him is so. In fact he was a khalifa in Bayt al-Maqdis in actuality, as the explicit wording requires through the use of ﴿fi﴾ (in). The unrestricted sense and the use of the definite article ﴿al-﴾ (the) point to the fact that it is the complete earth, because truth spread from it through Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his descendants over the rest of the earth. He is a khalifa over the whole earth potentially, in the sense that whatever he judges in it is valid. This is because the Prophet ﷺ was sent only to his own people, so what he conveys to them is obligatory for him. As for the rest of humanity, his dealing with them is by way of commanding good and forbidding evil (al-amr bil-ma'ruf wal-nahy 'anil-munkar), whatever he does of it is valid and stands. Then he was a khalifa over the whole earth in actuality, through his son Sulayman, peace be upon him. So he fulfilled the unrestrictedness and the definite article ﴿al-﴾, which completes the utmost that is intended by it, as notice that the speech of the All-Powerful is entirely like this, even if it does not appear in the present state. This is just as the one to whom this Reminder was sent down, and by whose means, Muhammad ﷺ, was a khalifa in actuality in the land of the Arabs, which is the whole earth, because the earth was spread out from it, and its House was the first house established for people, and it is a standing (qiyam) for them. From it the standing with light and justice spread over the whole earth, and it is potentially over the whole earth, in the sense that whatever he judged in it stands. He gave Tamim al-Dari, may Allah be pleased with him, the land of the town of the Friend (al-Khalil), from the lands of al-Sham, before it was conquered, and it was valid and executed. He gave Shuwayl, may Allah be pleased with him, the daughter of Buqayla from the people of al-Hira, and that was valid and executed. Each of them took what he had given him ﷺ at the conquest. Then he will be a khalifa over the whole earth in actuality, through his successor whom Allah strengthened with him in his religion, ʿIsa, peace be upon him, who is from the descendants of Dawud, peace be upon him. Then over all existence on the Day of Resurrection, the Day of the Great Intercession, the Day on which all the prophets will be under his banner, and the first and the last will envy him for that station of praise.

When the blessing was complete, He caused His saying to follow from it: ﴿So judge between the people﴾, that is, those who come to you for judgment from whatever people they are, ﴿with truth﴾, that is, the established matter to which reality conforms. Since the greatest enemy of a human being is his own soul that lies between his two sides, because of its desires, and the greatest of his crimes and the worst of his sins is what proceeds from it without basis in the command of Allah, He said, indicating by the form of the reflexive (ifti'al) that He, glorified is He, pardons the passing thoughts, and whatever the human being hastens to turn back from and to be free of, in repentance to Allah (Exalted): ﴿And do not follow desire﴾, that is, what makes its owner go astray, so that it casts him down from the height of good pleasure to the lowest pit of Satan. Then He caused His saying to follow from that: ﴿for it will lead you astray﴾, that is, that following or desire, because when the soul has become accustomed to that, it becomes a disposition for it, and so it overcomes its owner so that he cannot turn it back from that. He turned the speech from the locus of greatness to the Greatest Name, which gathers all the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes, magnifying the affair of His path and urging adherence to it and the honour of entering it.
