So He said: ﴿from the path of Allah﴾, that is, His way which He legislated for reaching Him, through what He sent down of transmitted revelation (naql), supported by the evidences of what He created of intellect ('aql). It is not reached without these, because following it requires absorption in bodily pleasures and neglect of the perfecting of the spiritual faculties, which lead to eternal happiness. For the impulses of the body and of the spirit are opposed, so the more one of them increases, the more the other decreases.

Since the soul is inclined toward desire and turns away from other than it, He said, giving the reason for the prohibition and emphasizing what the soul has of pretexts at the time of disobedience, with generosity and forgiveness that repel punishment: ﴿Indeed, those who go astray﴾, that is, who bring about error by their neglect of taqwa (God-consciousness), which necessitates following desire, which requires that its follower be astray, ﴿from the path of Allah﴾. He repeated it to exalt its matter, to seek blessing by mentioning it, and to announce that His path is commanded absolutely, without restriction to Dawud, peace be upon him, or anyone else in it. ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾, that is, because of their going astray.

When He, glorified is He, had commanded and forbidden, and had mentioned that the reason for the prohibition is the dislike of going astray, and it was known from this that the cause of going astray is desire, He mentioned the cause of this cause, saying, expressing it by forgetting (nisyan), indicating that because of its intense manifestness, just as it was preserved, it was forgotten. He used the verbal noun (maṣdar) in an unpacked form (fakk al-maṣdar) because it is more explicit, since if he had expressed it by the verbal noun it would have been possible to make it an attribution to the object. The particle ﹙ma﹚ was chosen over ﹙an﹚, because its form is the form of the substantive relative pronoun, and that is more eloquent than what is a particle in form and meaning: ﴿for that they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾, that is, they treated it as something forgotten, some by denial, and some by the wickedness of their deeds. For if they had truly remembered it, they would not have followed the desire that necessitates error. Moreover, it is something that no one with even the slightest grain of intellect is ignorant of, for it does not occur to any intelligent mind at all that the least and most ignorant of people would send someone to a farm of his that he is working, and then not call him to account for it, let alone when he is wise? How much more when he is a king? How much more when He is the King of kings?

Al-Ghazali said, at the end of the Book of Knowledge from the Revival of the Religious Sciences (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din), in discussing the intellect: Then, since faith is fixed in souls by nature (fitra), people divided into those who turned away and forgot, and they are the disbelievers, and those whose thought circulated and so they remembered, and that was like one who was entrusted with testimony, then forgot it through heedlessness, and then remembered it. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: "that perhaps they may remember" (la'allahum yatadhakkarun); ﴿and that those of understanding may remember﴾ [Sad 38:29]; ﴿and remember the blessing of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:7]; ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar 54:17]. Naming this type "remembrance" is not far-fetched. It seems that remembrance has two kinds: one is that a person recalls a form that was present in his heart but disappeared after being present; the other is that it is about a form that was included in him by nature. These are realities manifest to one who looks with the light of insight, and heavy for one who relies on hearing and imitation rather than unveiling and direct vision. End of quotation.

It is known from this story and what came before it that the meaning is: Be patient over what they say now, for We will surely support you in what comes in time, and We will strengthen you just as We strengthened Dawud, the one of great station.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 27:

Since the implied sense is: "We did not decree in eternity the Day of Reckoning, and We did not threaten with it, [and so] it would be in vain," He connected to it His saying, turning the speech away from the third person to the manifestation of majesty (ʿaẓamah), indicating that the Mighty, whose majesty requires it, does not [act] except with a mighty purpose: (p-371) ﴿And We did not create﴾, that is, in accordance with the majesty that belongs to Us. It is also permissible for the clause to be circumstantial (ḥāliyyah, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action): ﴿the heaven and the earth and what is between them﴾. Since the context concerns the discord that occurred out of obstinacy, not ignorance, He mentioned of the heavens what cannot be disputed, although the word is generic and so encompasses all of them. He said: ﴿the heaven﴾, that is, the one you see; ﴿and the earth and what is between them﴾, of what you perceive, such as the winds and other things, as a creation ﴿in vain﴾, that is, for no purpose that We intended by it, such as the reckoning of those in them, just as the least of you reckons those under him in terms of recompense, and repays those in them with reward for the one who obeys and punishment for the one who disobeys, as the least of your kings does. For the lowest of people in intellect does not construct a huge building except for a purpose he intends, and that purpose is the separation between people, those to whom We gave strength and capacity in this abode, and among whom We scattered the causes that necessitate the spread of clarity and turbidity, and to whom We gave intellects as a reminder of what is intended, and among whom We sent messengers and sent down books to them, informing them of what pleases Us and what angers Us. Yet they rejected all of that. Had We left them without gathering them [for judgment] or doing justice between them, this entire creation would have been in vain, with no wisdom in it at all, because its creation was either for harm, or for benefit, or for neither of these. The first is void, because it is unbefitting the Merciful, the Generous; the third is void, because it was so in the state of non-existence, so there remained no preponderant reason for bringing it into being. Thus the middle option is determined, which is benefit. This cannot be [the benefit] of this world, because its harm is greater than its benefit, and bearing much harm for little benefit (p-372) is unbefitting the Wise, the Generous. Therefore what is determined is that which the true promise has affirmed, the benefit of the Hereafter, which accords with what has been mentioned from the intellect of the intelligent and the conduct of the noble.

Since this, namely the rejection of wisdom, is very great, He magnified it by His saying: ﴿That﴾, that is, the matter far removed from correctness, ﴿is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾, that is, whoever brings this assumption into being at any time has indeed brought disbelief into being, because he has denied the wisdom, which is the resurrection, for the manifestation of the attributes of perfection, and the recompense with reward and punishment. Whoever denies wisdom has in fact belittled the Creator, so his affirmation that He is a Creator becomes like "no affirmation," and he is thus a disbeliever in Him. Then He stated as a consequence of this assumption His saying: ﴿So woe﴾, that is, great destruction because of this assumption. He used the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun, to generalize and to attach the ruling to the attribute, saying: ﴿to those who disbelieved﴾, that is, absolutely, in this assumption and in other than it, ﴿from﴾, that is, beginning from ﴿the Fire﴾, that is, the ruling against them by it.

Since the implied sense was: "Shall We create that in vain, so that it has no outcome in which His wisdom appears, while We are exempt from futility?", he followed it with His words, as a denunciation of what follows from abandoning the resurrection, namely equating between things whose nature demands differentiation; and that is worse than futility, though He is able to do so, since nothing is ugly from Him: ﴿Or shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾; that is, despite our greatness; ﴿those who believe﴾; that is, obeying Our commands (p-373); ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾; that is, confirming their claim of faith; ﴿righteous deeds﴾ from among the actions; ﴿like those who cause corruption and do evil deeds?﴾ Or shall We make the reformers in the earth ﴿like the corrupters﴾; that is, those disposed to corruption and firmly established in it; ﴿in the earth﴾; that is, through disbelief and other things. Equating them is folly, and no rational person doubts that. ﴿Or shall We make﴾, by virtue of the might and protection We possess, those who are mindful of God ﴿like the wicked﴾? Or shall We place ﴿the God-conscious﴾; that is, the firmly rooted among the believers in the piety that requires refraining from everything not indicated by evidence; ﴿like the profligate﴾; that is, those who leave the circle of piety without restraint, from among these disbelievers or from others; in that each of those mentioned lives according to what their state led them to in this world; and usually the life of the wicked is loftier than the life of the righteous; then they die and nothing comes after that? There is no doubt that equating the reformer with the corrupter, and the God-conscious with the profligate, is something no wise person, nor any other kind of rational being, would accept. He, glory be to Him, does not do it, though He is able to, since nothing is obligatory upon Him and nothing is ugly from Him.

It is known that the verse is of the type of *ihtibak* (interlocking ellipsis), and that it points to another *ihtibak*: He mentioned "those who believe" first, as an indication of "those who corrupt" second, and mentioned "the corrupters" second, as an indication of "the believers" first. The mention of "those who are mindful of God" and their opposites conveys this. The secret of what was mentioned and what was omitted is that He mentioned the lowest rank of faith, to alert to its nobility and that it is the cause of happiness, even if at its minimal level; and He mentioned the highest states of corruption, to indicate that He forgives what is below that for whomever He wills; and He mentioned the highest states of piety, hinting that it is not described by it, nor deserving of its reward, except for the one firmly rooted in it, as encouragement for the believer to strive to ascend to its heights.

When what has been mentioned from the beginning of the surah until here, of the proofs mentioned in this Reminder, which none but a mind of corrupted reasoning and confused intellect would reject, was established, it became clear that it is the Possessor of the Reminder and of the greatest nobility. So He (Exalted is He) said, alerting to this, indicating that it is the canon by which righteousness is known so that it may be followed, and corruption so that it may be avoided, informing about a subject whose predicate (mubtada', subject) is estimated as "He is": ﴿A Book﴾; that is, it has from greatness that which cannot be encompassed. He described it by His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you﴾; that is, with what We possess of greatness; ﴿to you﴾; and that is from its greatness, because you are the greatest of creation. Then He informed about another subject, clarifying what came before it, by way of resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence), so He said: ﴿Blessed﴾; that is, constant in good, abundant in benefit, and everything in it is established with an establishment that never ceases, ever; and no book nor anything abrogates it.

When He mentioned what it possesses of greatness, both by allusion and by expression, He mentioned the ultimate purpose of its sending down, which was commanded, so He said: ﴿that they may ponder﴾ with the letter ta' (in the second person, yatadabbaru becoming tadabbaru) and with the lightening of the dal, in the address form, in the recitation of Abu Ja'far (qira'ah, a canonical reading), honouring the Ummah by joining them in address to his exalted presence (ﷺ); and drawing attention to the speech, in the recitation of the community (the majority), in the third person with the doubling of the dal, to those who need to be alerted to the causes, because of the preoccupations that cause disorder. As for him (ﷺ), he is in the utmost of favour for reflection and contemplation with the clearest thoughts, from the moment of sending down, because of his knowledge of the cause of the sending down; to the extent that, because of the severity of its fatiguing of his noble self, he was commanded to lighten it, and (Exalted is He) guaranteed to him its gathering and its recitation (Qur'an). ﴿His verses﴾; that is, so that they may look into the consequences of every verse, and what it leads to and conveys of inner meanings, which prolonged reflection upon the outward has made known. Whoever is content with confining himself to memorising its letters is like one who has a milch-cow yielding milk that he does not milk, or a mare that bears foals that he does not breed; and he is deserving of losing its limits, so that he suffers manifest loss.

Since every person is commanded to be alert, through everything he sees and hears, to what lies behind it, and it was not within the capacity of every person to reach the end of that, He was content from them with what falls short of it; so the ta' of the tafa''ul form (the reflexive pattern, a grammatical conjugation) was assimilated into the first root letter of the word, as an indication of that; as the recitation of Abu Ja'far indicates it. Perhaps the recitation of the community indicates striving in understanding its hidden meanings; and God knows best.

Since the context is that of remembrance, and it is ascribed to the essence of creation, and since recalling what a person had and forgot is not difficult, because it is evident, He made the ta' explicit, urging exertion in employing thought and persevering in that; for it leads, after the premises that are conjectural, to matters that are certain and definite, either perceptible, or having a witness in sense perception. So He said: ﴿and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾; that is, after reflection, a great and clear remembrance, by what the explicitness has indicated; ﴿those of understanding﴾; that is, of everything it guides to, of what God has made known to them in themselves and in the horizons; for they find that known to them by sense or otherwise, in themselves or in other than themselves. Nothing in the Qur'an departs from consideration of something known to a human being, about which he has no dispute at all; but God (Exalted is He) manifests it to whom He wills and conceals it from whom He wills: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves﴾; and its most manifest form is on the Day of Resurrection, for it is fixed in the nature of every person that the leader does not leave those under his hand without any reckoning at all.

Since a person, however long he reflects and however fully he turns himself to remembrance, must inevitably experience forgetfulness, heedlessness and distraction; and since the one who is praised is only the one who returns (to God) often, as in the hadith: "«“If you did not sin, God would bring a people who sin, then they would seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them.”»"; and since God (exalted) is the King who has no partner, and the Owner to whom all dominion belongs, He raises [p. 377] whom He wills, from among those who would never occur to anyone to be raised, and He lowers whom He wills, from among those who have risen in dominion to the point that it never enters the mind that any defect could befall them, especially if they were at the highest level of obedience. This is so that He makes clear to every person of understanding that the one who does this is the Chooser who acts freely, so that His goodness is always hoped for and His retribution is always feared and dreaded. God (exalted) said: ﴿And We bestowed﴾, that is, by what We have of wisdom and greatness, ﴿upon Dawud, Sulayman﴾, so he came, in that time, unmatched in that regard, in religion, in worldly affairs, in knowledge, in wisdom, in forbearance, in greatness and in mercy. For this reason He drew attention to the likes of these meanings by resuming the report about what moved the soul to ask about them, namely the attribution of the bestowing to the nun of majesty (the "we" form of divine self-reference), so He said: ﴿What an excellent servant﴾. And since the context concerns the swift awakening from heedlessnesses, the release from lapses, the repentance from slips, and the clarification that trial is not confined to punishments but may be for the elevation of ranks, and since this is far from customary, he gave the reason for his praise, emphasizing it with His saying: ﴿Indeed he was one who turns back (awwab)﴾, that is, one who returns to increasing striving in exceeding gratitude and in patience under affliction, every time he rises from a station, by seeking forgiveness from it, and counting it, along with all the perfection he has, among what is to be turned away from.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 31:

When horses were among the greatest of the things adorned for people from the love of desires, and the context concerned might (ʿizzah) and opposition (shiqāq), which indicate the great need for that which restrains these things, of which horses are the greatest, He mentioned in this regard a command to him (ﷺ), which indicates that, despite the greatness of his kingdom, he was greatly given to returning (to God) and was great in it, because whoever did not have that as a natural disposition would not have been able to do what he did. So He said: ﴿When﴾, meaning: remember, so that you may witness the evidence of what We have told you, at the time when ﴿there were displayed before him, in the evening﴾, meaning: after the sun had passed its zenith, ﴿the poised steeds﴾, meaning: the pure Arab horses, which can hardly keep all their legs firmly on the ground, out of self-admiration, and because of their closeness to flying, owing to their lightness and their high spirit, and to show their strength, their grace and their agility. In al-Qamus it says: "ṣafana al-faras yaṣfanu ṣufūnan": he stood on three legs with the tip of the hoof of the fourth touching the ground. Al-Qazzaz said: he stood on three legs, and raised a leg from the ground, or the tip of its hoof touched the ground in order to rest by that; and horses most often do this when they are noble (ʿitāq). He said: It is said that every hoofed animal does this, but among the swift horses it is more common, and it hardly occurs except in pure-bred Arab horses. It is also said: "al-ṣāfin" is one who joins his two forelegs and bends the tip of the hoof of one of his hind legs; and it is said: "al-ṣāfin" is one who raises the hoof of one of his forelegs; and when he raises the tip of the hoof of one of his hind legs, he is then called "mukhayyim," and it is said "qad akhāma" when he does that.

When it became clear that it is permissible to interpret "al-ṣāfin" as applying to a non-noble horse, though this is rare, he clarified that the intended meaning is the description of excellence, whether standing or running, so He said: ﴿the swift ones﴾, meaning: those which excel in their running with the utmost of what they are capable of, plural of "jawād." (p-379) They kept being displayed before him until the prayer of the end of the day had passed him by; and what was obligatory upon those before us was two rak'ahs at the beginning of the day and two rak'ahs at its end, so he immediately repented.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 32:

When the explanation of the greatness of his kingdom, the abundance of his awe and might, and the increase in his return (to God) had been given, so that consolation might be found in his good obedience and his conclusion, and solace in his trial, along with what was in him of nobility and splendour, (God) pointed to the very great number of the horses and the increase in his love for them and the speed of his return by His saying: ﴿He said﴾. Since what was fitting for his condition, and what was known of his deeds, was that he would not prefer anything over the remembrance of God, scarcely would anyone who witnessed that suspect this of him. Rather, they would give him various interpretations in this matter and would attribute to him meanings fitting to what they knew of his state of turning to God and being free of anything other than Him. He (God) emphasised his saying, out of humility before God (exalted is He), so that they would believe that he is a human being to whom what is permitted for them is permitted, were it not for God's protection: ﴿Indeed I﴾. Since love is an inward matter that does not appear in anything except through a great deal of occupation with it, and since occupation may be for other than love, so that it does not indicate it except through indicators, he said, by way of acknowledgement: ﴿have loved﴾, that is: I brought into being and made manifest, by what appeared from me of occupation with the horses, this being accompanied by evidences of affection, ﴿the love of good﴾ (p-380), which is wealth, indeed the essence of wealth and the cause of every good, worldly and otherworldly: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection." I manifested that with the utmost desire, heedless of ﴿the remembrance of my Lord﴾, who had done good to me by these horses, which occupied me and other things, so I did not remember Him with the prayer that was the duty of the time, although my purpose in it was, because it was in His obedience, a remembrance of Him. That state continued with me ﴿until it was hidden﴾, that is: the sun, which is understood from "the evening," ﴿behind the veil﴾, which is the earth that came between us and it, so that it was in fact behind it.

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on surah 38, verse 33:

When the listener's eagerness for the act that earned him the description "oft-returning" (awwab) grew intense, after hearing his words in blaming himself, so that he might combine knowledge of the speech and of the deed, he was answered with His words: ﴿Bring them back to me﴾. That is, Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "Bring back to me ﴿the horses﴾ which distracted me." Since the intended meaning was "so they brought them back to him," he linked to it His words: ﴿So he began﴾. That is, he set about doing it, achieving his aim, persisting in it, committed to it, reaching it, relying on God for strengthening against the enemy, and not on the means, the greatest of which is horses, abandoning what had been the cause of his heedlessness of the remembrance, turning away from whatever the heart might become attached to, drawing near to God (Exalted) by it, just as one draws near in this religion (p-381) by sacrifices. ﴿Striking﴾: that is, he inflicted the striking, i.e., the cutting, upon them with the sword, in a mighty manner. Since the sword only falls upon a small part of the two limbs, he introduced the preposition bi-, saying: ﴿on the legs﴾, that is, of them, ﴿and the necks﴾: he strikes them with a sharp sword, a strong arm and sound workmanship, passing through them without any pause at all, until it is as though he were wiping over the surface of their hides, as one says: "he wiped his neck," that is, he struck his neck. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 34:

When there became evident through this the great extent of his kingdom and the might of his sovereignty, and the turning back (awba) was very great, and steadfastness upon the station of witnessing (shuhud), together with his being guarded from all his aspects, was greater, He drew attention to it by His saying, emphasizing what souls are disposed to, namely the assumption that one who turns back (awwab) should not be confronted with reproach: ﴿And We did test﴾, i.e., by what We possess of greatness; ﴿Solomon﴾, i.e., together with his hastening to return to God and his alertness to what pleases Him, a kind of trial, God knows best its reality. So that trial resulted in his firm establishment in the station of turning back, so he became alert to what We intended by it of training him in what We had established him in, just as We did with his father David, peace be upon them both. So follow their example in taking insight from trial, for indeed We intend for you a great, exalted, noble and generous matter. ﴿And We cast﴾, i.e., by what We possess of greatness; ﴿upon his throne﴾, which the lions of the thicket used to fear.

Since the lesson is only in meanings, whoever has a deficient meaning is like a body without a soul, having a form without a meaning; He said: ﴿a body﴾. So that noble place was overcome by it, in spite of what We had honoured him with of the awe of prophethood combined with kingship, to the extent that no one imagined that anyone could approach him, let alone overcome him. So We enabled this body over him with an enablement in which there was no hardship upon him; rather it was such that it was as if it had been cast upon him without his choice, so that he would know that the kingdom belongs only to Us; We do what We will with whom We will. Happiness is for whoever hopes in Us, and woe to whoever feels secure from Our plan and so does not fear Us. Soon this city will be in your grip, and its people, despite their might and dissension, will be obedient to your will; and there will be for you by that an authority that will not be for anyone after you, just as no one before you had such command, such might, such grandeur, such settlement in the sacred precinct to the extent of need, such breadth of kingdom, and such enduring remembrance. What you are in now is a trial, a test, and a training for the great matters that are to come.

Since the intended meaning of applying the term "body" to him is to define that it has no meaning, not that it has no soul, He applied it without following it with anything that shows it to be inanimate, as He did with the calf, where He said: "It had a lowing" (khuwar); thereby He made clear that it had no soul. And if it is sound that this body was Sakhr the jinn, and that its cause was the prostration of the jarada, the wife of Solomon, peace be upon him, to the image of her father, without the knowledge of the Prophet of God Solomon, peace be upon him, nor his will, then the indication in this, as consolation, is that We stripped the kingdom from Our chosen one because of an image that some of those ascribed to him had raised, in his house, prostrating to it, without his command, nor his will, nor his knowledge; so how about those who prostrate to these idols in the Sacred House?! Soon We shall remove their affair, quench their evil, and erase their remembrance.

Since repentance (inabah) is a return to what was, it is a recovery of what was lost; He said: ﴿Then he turned back﴾;

He explained the repentance (inabah) so that it would be known that He (exalted be He) tested him, even though he was a servant of great station whose supplication is answered. This is by his saying, in answer to one who asked about it: ﴿My Lord﴾; that is, O You who are good to me; ﴿forgive me﴾; that is, the matter because of which the repentance was. When he had mentioned the matter of the Hereafter, he followed it with his saying: ﴿and grant me﴾; that is, specifically for me; ﴿a kingdom that is not fitting﴾; that is, its request is not found in such a way that obedience and ease are obtained with it, ﴿for anyone﴾; at any time, whether long or short; whether it is complete in form and meaning, or a body devoid of power, as the trial had occurred through it before. He made the time specific by mentioning the preposition, so he said: ﴿after me﴾; so that I may be able to do everything that is desired of nearness to You and of fighting those who oppose You, and so that this would be a sign for me of the acceptance of my repentance, and no trial would befall me by placing something upon the seat of my judgment or elsewhere. This indicates that the trial was in the kingdom. Likewise, the mention of the placing upon the throne, attributed to it, without attributing anything to him (peace be upon him), is appropriate to the hamstringing of the horses, which is the removal of what held power. And God knows best. By this estimation it is known that had he mentioned the time without a particle, it would have implied that the supplication was restricted to a kingdom that would extend over the time after him. Then he gave the reason for what he asked of giving and withholding by his saying, as an emphasis, dropping what dominates souls of seeing the causes: ﴿Indeed You, You﴾; that is, You alone; ﴿are the Bestower﴾; that is, the one of great gifts; with the repetition, whenever You wish, so You give by means and without means to whom You will, and withhold from whom You will.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 36:

When his supplication had its answer as a consequence, Allah—glorified is He—informed of it by His saying: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind﴾; that is, We made it submissive, by what We have of majesty; ﴿to him the wind﴾, to strike terror into the enemy and to attain objectives, in exchange for the horses which he gave up for Our sake. Then He explained the subjection by His saying, in a resumptive manner: ﴿running gently by his command﴾; that is, while it was extremely gentle in its softness, obedient, by which is attained what cannot be attained with horses; ﴿its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [Saba': 12]. Whoever leaves something for the sake of Allah, Allah replaces it for him with something better than it. Here, "rukhā'" (gentle, soft) is an intensive form of "rakhāwah" (softness). And since its reaching whatever he wills was inseparable from his will, he expressed it by that, because it is the thing intended in itself; so He said: ﴿wherever he directed it﴾; that is, wherever he willed to reach any of the things. Allah had given our Prophet ﷺ something greater than that, which is that the enemy would be struck with terror from him at a distance of a month's journey from each of his four sides; so these are four months.

And the devils (We subjected to him), namely those who possess lightness of wind together with the quality of being bound to the spirit; We subjected them to him. Then he drew attention to their benefit by substitution from them, saying: ﴿every﴾, and he expressed it with the intensive pattern in the context of favour, saying: ﴿builder and diver﴾; that is, great in building, rising into the atmosphere of the sky, and diving down into the depths of the water, extracting pearls and other benefits of the sea.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 38, verse 38:

When He indicated the general subjugation of them, He indicated that it was by compulsion and dominance, as is the manner of the governance of kingship and the assault of might. So He said: ﴿And others﴾; that is, We subjugated them for him from among the devils, being ﴿bound together﴾ by His command with those who resemble them; or their hands being bound to their feet, or to their necks. He expressed it with the intensive form (muqarrinin) rather than "muqarinin," for example, to indicate the severity of their fetters and the great extent of their binding. And since these fetters prevented them from exercising control over themselves, they were treated as though all of them were in them, even though only some of their limbs were in them, like "they put their fingers in their ears." So He said: ﴿in shackles﴾; that is, the bonds with which captives are bound, of iron or of a chain or other than that; it is the plural of "ṣafad" (ṣafad, a shackle), with a vowel on the ṣād. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) (p-386) said: "Indeed an 'ifrit (ʿifrīt, a powerful jinn) from among the jinn slipped up on me last night in order to cut off my prayer, but Allah enabled me to overcome him, so I seized him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that all of you could look at him, but I remembered the supplication of my brother Solomon: 'My Lord, grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me,' so I sent him back in disgrace." And Allah had given him authority over some of the jinn, so he was protected from those who attack the abode of his birth and the abode of his emigration. Ahmad related in his Musnad, with a sound chain (if Allah wills), from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Madinah and Makkah are surrounded by angels; at every passage of each of them is an angel, so the Dajjal will not enter them, nor the plague." This applies to the two cities; as for Madinah specifically, there are many hadiths about it from several Companions, in the two Sahihs and others. Allah compensated our Prophet (ﷺ) for the devils with support through hosts of angels in his campaigns; and our Prophet was a servant, as he chose, so he had no need of anything other than that.

When this was a great kingdom, he drew attention to its greatness by its abundance, its permanence, and the greatness of the One who grants it. He then said, resuming the speech (*mustani'an*, introducing a new sentence), with an implied "We said to him" or similar: ﴿This is Our gift﴾. That is, this great matter is Our gift, according to the greatness that belongs to Us. Then, as a consequence of this, he mentioned (p. 387) the unrestricted disposal, which is the greatest of aims. For how many a possessor of something is still with his hand chained from disposing of it? So he said, beginning with what calls forth love and draws hearts, indicating His greatness and the manifestation of His command through *fakk al-idgham* (the unmerging of the doubled consonant, i.e., writing the doubled letter separately rather than assimilating it): ﴿so bestow, or withhold﴾. That is, give to whomever You wish as a gift, beginning without any cause from the recipient; or withhold from whomever You wish.

Since this gift is of a greatness that exceeds description, He increased its magnitude by its abundance, its ease, and the safety of its outcome, and so He said: ﴿without reckoning﴾. That is, all of this, the giving and the bestowing, is occurring free of *hisab* (reckoning). You do not fear any deficiency in it, for your Lord is the Giver and the Commander, nor do you fear that it will be something you are questioned about in the Hereafter, because He has permitted you. Thus the negation of reckoning concerning it conveys two things: abundance, and the absence of any overtaking in giving or withholding. Making it a *maṣdar mazīd* (a verbal noun of an augmented form) conveys that what is negated is only a reckoning that is counted and taken into account, not every kind of "reckoning" (*ḥisāb*) by estimation, such as occurs with things that baffle the one who attempts to count them, so that their matter approaches by a kind of conjecture.

When He had lifted the burden from him in both abodes, He affirmed the additional, saying, coordinating with what is implied by "This is for him in this world," and emphasizing an increase in reassurance, since it is an exception to what the customary rule had decreed, namely that whatever exceeds sufficiency (al-kafaf) in this world is deficient in one's share in the Hereafter (p-388): "And indeed for him, with Us, is a nearness" (ﷺ-less note: the Qur'anic text reads) ﴿And indeed, for him, with Us, is nearness (zulfa)﴾, meaning: specifically for him; ﴿with Us﴾, meaning: in the Hereafter; ﴿is a nearness﴾, meaning: a great closeness; ﴿and a good return﴾, meaning: a place of return.

When the account of the king who turned often (to God), who in actuality possessed the world by force, domination and victory, east and west, was finished, and Ayyub (peace be upon him) was in the prosperity of kings, though he was not a king in actuality, and the denial of whoever denied the Prophet (ﷺ) was only through God's empowering the devils over them by His whisperings, and His command, glorified is He, to be patient in that, and He related to him some of the accounts of those who turn often (to God), as a lesson in the goodness of returning (to God) should patience weaken, He followed it with the report about the patient one who turns often (to God), who did not complain except from the whispering of Satan to his wife, by what he used to tempt her with, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would increase in patience through remembering these accounts, and his turning to God (Exalted is He) and his humble supplication to Him would be multiplied, following the example of his brothers whom neither the gift of ease nor the affliction of hardship distracted from Him, and as a reminder of God's power over everything He wills, an alert that He is able to turn back Quraysh from what they are in, and to give victory to the weak among His servants over them, with the least effort. So He said: ﴿And mention Our servant﴾; that is, the one who is worthy of being attributed to Our great presence; and He specified him by saying: ﴿Ayyub﴾; and he was from the Romans, from the descendants of Eesau ibn Ishaq (peace be upon them), so that you may take him as a model in his condition, and be patient with your people, and if you see what you have no patience for, you should call upon God to set it right.

When He commanded him to mention him, He made clear that the main purpose is some of his noble conditions, so that he would take him as a model. He said, substituting it with a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition): ﴿when﴾; that is, mention his condition when he ﴿called out﴾; and he turned the speech away from the aspect of greatness toward the attribute of kindness, because that is its place, given what his condition required; so He said: ﴿to his Lord﴾, that is, the One who was good to him, whose goodness to him in nurturing him through His trials he recognized, just as he recognized His favor through the apparent blessings and bounties; then He mentioned what he called out with, relating it in his own words, and He said, indicating by the emphasis that he, although his condition in what was known of his great patience required not complaining, had been visited by what he had no patience for: ﴿Indeed I﴾; that is, my Lord, I call upon You because I. Since this was in the context of encouraging patience, He magnified the matter by attributing the harm to the greatest of enemies, as a spur toward answering, and as courtesy toward God; so He said: ﴿The devil has touched me﴾; that is, while I am among Your friends; ﴿the devil﴾; that is, the one burned by the curse, far from mercy, by Your empowering him over me; ﴿with hardship﴾; that is, harm, hardship, distress, illness, pain, and affliction that weighs heavily on its bearer, so that it tires him, wearies him, exhausts him, exhausts him with effort, and brings him to the utmost limit of all of that. It was also read with a ḍamma on the ṣād (nuṣ̲b̲), and read with a vocalic movement (naṣab), like ﴿ar-rushd﴾ and ﴿ar-rashad﴾. This indicated the degrees of harm in severity and lightness: the sukūn (quiescent form) is its lowest, the moved form is its middle, and the heavy form with ḍamma is its highest. ﴿And torment﴾; that is, a very strong, very intense, enduring distress, preventing from every pleasure, or that could be tasted, its finest part, and He made it indefinite to magnify it, while its brevity sufficed (for magnification) without long sentences and an extended supplication, informing that the flood has reached the top (of the hill) and affliction has weakened strength. He did not mention it with the word Iblis, which carries the meaning of despair and cutting off hope, as an indication that he himself was hoping for God's bounty, not despairing of His mercy. That is because God (Exalted is He) empowered him over destroying his family, his children and his wealth, and he was patient; then He empowered him over his body, until his flesh fell away, and this continued for long periods. Therefore, his wife, may God be pleased with her, appeared to him in the guise of a physician, and said to him: "I will treat you, and I want nothing except that when you are healed you say to me: 'You have healed me.'" It was said that he said to her: "If he prostrates to me one prostration, I will heal him." So she came to him and told him of that, and he informed her, and made her aware that it was Satan, and warned her against him, and feared his harm to her; so he called upon God with what has preceded, and intensified the rejection and the magnification of what he had whispered to her, by swearing that he would strike her one hundred blows, as a deterrent against her listening to anything of that, and a belittling of what he would suffer of his affliction in his body.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 42:

When the listener was eager to hear the answer to that, He resumed with His words: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾; that is, We said to him: strike the earth, and bring about the rukd (running/stamping), which is walking, moving, hastening, and urging on, ﴿with your foot﴾; from it will come forth water that is beneficial and good, so that you may bathe in it and drink from it. So he did it, and We caused a spring to gush forth for him. Then it was said to him: ﴿This﴾, with the demonstrative of nearness, indicating its ease, ﴿is a cool bath﴾; that is, water with which one bathes, and its place and its time are ﴿cool﴾; that is, it cools the heat of the outward body; ﴿and a drink﴾; which cools the heat of the inward body.

(p-٣٩٢)

Since the implied sequence was: "So he did it; he washed, and his outward body was healed and his inward self was gladdened," He joined to it His saying, turning the speech toward the manifestation of majesty to draw attention to the greatness of the act: ﴿And We gave﴾; that is, by what We possess of greatness; ﴿to him his family﴾; that is, those whom Satan had been empowered over, by Our reviving them; and He used the plural in consideration of the meaning, because it is more impressive and closer to conveying the intended sense. So He said: ﴿and their like﴾. And He made known that they were all gathered together at one time, so He said: ﴿along with them﴾. We renewed them for him, and so that whoever hears of this may know that there is no true value in anything of this world, and that it, and everything in it, is a passing accident with no permanence at all, except what belongs to Us, for that is among "the enduring good deeds" (al-baqiyat al-salihat). Therefore no one should be diverted by anything of it, nor should anyone be preoccupied with it to the exclusion of Us at all. From this, whoever affirms Him will know His power to resurrect merely by his affirming Him, and whoever hesitates about it should ask the People of the Scripture (Ahl al-Kitab, the Jews and Christians), and he will know it through their confirmation of it. Then He, glorified is He, gave the reason for that act by His saying: ﴿as a mercy﴾. And since the context is one of urging patience, He magnified the matter by His saying: ﴿from Us﴾, for it is greater than the expression in Surat al-Anbiya' (The Prophets), ﴿with Us﴾ (ʿindana), so that this would be more compelling in holding fast to patience. If you look at the endings of the two verses, you will recognize the difference between the two expressions, and it will become clear to you that the station of patience is not equal to anything, because the path to Him, glorified is He, is never free of patience, of restraining the self, and of compulsion, since the self, by consensus, opposes what the natural inclinations call for. ﴿And a reminder﴾; that is, an honour, and a great admonition; ﴿for those of understanding﴾; that is, those of pure intellects. We made that a sign of His mercy, and a reminder to others among those described, across long periods of time, so that every one who is tested may take him as an example and hope for what he hoped for, for the mercy of God is vast, and He is near to broken hearts. Between a servant and the answer there is nothing but the goodness of turning back (to Him). Whoever keeps turning to Him constantly, He will suffice him against all others:

*For everything, when you part from it, there is a substitute,*
*but for God, if you part from Him, there is no substitute.*

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 44:

When He had summarily mentioned the painful punishment, the suffering of the outward body, and mentioned the means of deliverance from it, He followed this with an alert to its greatest form, which is the suffering of the inward self, or rather the innermost of the inward: the attachment to belief in what was whispered to his wife, may Allah be pleased with her, by which he (Satan) nearly caused her to slip. So he swore that he would strike her one hundred times, lest she return to anything of that kind and thereby cause her to slip from her station, as he had caused others to slip. Glorified and exalted is He, guided him to a way out of that oath, in the lightest manner, because she had been patient and virtuous. Allah thanked her for that, and made this way out after her a lasting practice (sunnah) for His servants, as a magnification of her reward and a good remembrance of her. So He said, conjoining it (by ʿatf) to ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Ṣād 38:42]: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍighth)﴾, that is, the hand which had come to the utmost health; ﴿a bundle﴾, that is, a small bundle of grass containing one hundred stalks, like the stalk of a palm frond. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is whatever you gather of anything, such as a moist bundle. Al-Samīn said: the root of the word indicates the gathering of mixed things. ﴿Then strike with it﴾, that is, a striking of any kind, one stroke. ﴿And do not break your oath﴾, that is, do not sin by leaving what you swore to do. This is a lightening for both of them because of his patience. Perhaps the expiation (kaffārah) was not among them, and Allah singled us out with it, along with His legislation for us, as an honour to us, as to how much He made it lenient for him. All of this is an announcement that Allah, exalted is He, tested him, peace and blessings be upon him, in his body, his children, and his wealth, and nothing remained to him but a wife, so Satan whispered to her, desiring to harm them both, just as he had harmed Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, peace be upon them both, until he came close to some of what he wanted. The purpose of informing him of this is to remind the Prophet (ﷺ) that if He empowered Satan to whisper to his relatives, to mislead and to misguide, then He has bestowed upon him his wife, the greatest of the ministers of truthfulness, and many of his relatives, the paternal uncles, the sons of paternal uncles, and others, and He preserved for him his body and his wealth, so that his gratitude to Allah, exalted is He, might increase. In the story there is also an indication that He is able to make subject to him whomever He wills, for He is capable of disposing of meanings just as He is capable of disposing of essences. And He, glorified is He, will grant this noble Prophet his people, the Arabs, who are now the fiercest of people against him, and others, so that all of them will obey him.

Since patience and pleasing deeds are rare among servants, and are hardly ever found, it is hardly believed that they exist. Glorified is He gave a reason for this honour to him (ﷺ) and affirmed it, saying, by way of deduction from what preceded, as a rebuttal to whoever thinks that complaining to Him contradicts patience, and as an indication that the secret of reminding him of it is to take him as an example in patience: ﴿Indeed We﴾, that is, with what We have of greatness; ﴿found him﴾, that is, in the world of witnessing, in accordance with what was ours in the world of the unseen, so that knowledge of that might become renewed for people, of what We had known. And since the context was an exhortation to patience in general, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:10], He used the active participle without intensification, saying: ﴿patient (ṣābiran)﴾. Then He resumed with His saying: ﴿an excellent servant (niʿma al-ʿabd)﴾. Then He gave a reason with His saying, affirming (it), lest it be thought that his trial detracts from that: ﴿Indeed he is one who repeatedly turns (awwāb)﴾, that is, one who returns wholly to Allah, glorified is He, contrary to what human nature calls for. Al-Rāzī said in Al-Lawāmiʿ: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: he stands with us with good manners; the continuance of blessing does not alter him, and the continuous succession of trial and affliction does not disturb him. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated in his Musnad, from Abū Saʿīd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A man placed his hand on the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'By Allah, I cannot bear to place my hand on you because of the intensity of your fever.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed we, the company of the prophets, have our trial doubled just as our reward is doubled. If a prophet among the prophets is tested with lice until it kills him, and if a prophet among the prophets is tested with poverty until he takes a cloak and wraps himself in it, and indeed they used to rejoice in trial just as they rejoice in ease.'"

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the one whom He tested in his body, his wealth, and his children, and then made water for him cool, safe, a source of wellbeing, order, healing and sustenance, He followed it with the one whom He tested with fire at the hands of the tyrants. He made the fire cool and safe for him because of his reliance on Him and his patience with Him, and He saved him from their scheming, and made his strength, alone, prevail over their strength. Then He tested him with emigration from his homeland, his family, his kinsfolk and his dwelling, and then with the slaughter of his son. He endured all of that, relying on Allah's grace and bounty. So He said: ﴿And remember Our servant﴾ in the singular (tawhid), according to the reading of Ibn Kathir. The word may be taken as a generic noun, or as referring to Ibrahim alone, peace be upon him, because he is the origin of those who are joined to him in religion and in fatherhood. Thus Allah clarified the basis of their being joined to him in praise, namely servanthood. Then He explained the intended meaning of His words ﴿Ibrahim﴾. He joined the rest to "servant" and not to the explanatory term, so that it would not follow that one explanation is joined to a group when only Ibrahim alone is intended and not the genus. His son (is joined) because of his patience in his religion while a stranger among the worshippers of idols and those far from faith. He did not turn to their ways or draw near to them, but was sent to his relatives in (p-396) the lands of the East, and he married from among them whoever agreed with him in the true religion. He persisted in sincere worship, not fearing the blame of any blamer for the sake of Allah, until he passed on to his Lord. So He said: ﴿and Ishaq﴾. Then He followed him with his son, who trod in his footsteps and bore patiently as he did, and who was tested by the loss of his son and the joy of his heart. He endured the most complete patience in that hardship, and offered the most eloquent praise and thanks. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿and Yaqub﴾. He joined the two of them to their father, glory be to Him, after the reading in the singular had shown the primacy of his (Ibrahim's) status in praise through servanthood. So He joined them to Himself in the reading other than that of Ibn Kathir: "Our servants" in the plural, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith - We will join their offspring with them﴾ [al-Tur: 21].

When they were gathered together by conjunction or apposition, He described them with His words ﴿those of strength (ayd) and vision (absar)﴾. That is, those of great power and sound deeds, because hands are the greatest instruments of that. ﴿And vision﴾ means the outer and inner senses, which are worthy of being mentioned and praised for them, because of the strength of their perception and the greatness of their penetration into what is worthy of being observed of the majesty of Allah and of watchfulness over movements and stillnesses, secretly and openly. He expressed this by "vision" because it is the strongest of its sources. Whoever is not like them is deprived of strength and intellect, and so has no real intellect, and is thus as nothing. Therefore it is the greatest rebuke to whoever Allah has given strength and intellect, yet does not direct them to the worship of Allah and striving in Him, glory be to Him. (p-397)

Al-Biqa'i's commentary (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 46:

When the listener's eagerness to learn what earned them this mention had become intense, He said, emphasizing it to indicate His love for their praise and to refute anyone who attributes to them, or to any one of them, what is unseemly, just as the Jews denied this in what they altered of the Tawrah (Torah) concerning Ishaq (Isaac), peace be upon him, in some passages. He made the verb transitive with the hamza (the alif of transitivity, *al-hamza*), to indicate that He drew them away from obstacles toward Himself with a single pull, one that is extremely swift: ﴿Indeed, We purified them﴾. That is, a purification for Us that is befitting of Our greatness, to which no greatness is comparable. ﴿With a pure quality﴾: that is, deeds, states, stations, trials, and afflictions that are free from any admixture, so that by enduring patiently through them they attained the utmost purity.

Since the cause of this purification is the remembrance of the Day of Judgment, and what becomes manifest on it of the attributes of majesty and beauty, and what is revealed on it of matters whose greatness cannot be described, He explained it by His saying: ﴿The remembrance of the Home﴾. That is, that pure quality reminds them, with a great reminder that never leaves them at all, of the Home that nothing else deserves to be called a home in any respect. So much so that, through the remembrance of this unseen reality, they forget the remembrance of what they witness of the home of this world; they do not look at it at all, out of hatred for it. Thus this unseen, enduring reality has made them forget the visible, perishing one, the reverse of what the common people hold.

The reading of Nafi', Abu Ja'far, and Hisham (on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, with a variant from him) of the phrase *bi-khalisah* (with the feminine adjective) as an idafa (genitive construction) supports what I have said: that *dhikra* is an explanation, since it is the attribution of the attribute to the thing it describes. The meaning is that they do nothing except that it is (p-٣٩٨) bringing them closer to the Hereafter. So the meaning is that their remembrance of it is pure, free from anything else, not shared by anything, and not mixed with any admixture at all.

When this sentence pointed to this eloquent praise, He followed it with what is inseparable from sincerity. Emphasizing what had preceded, as a reminder that they are among those who are to be envied for being praised, and as a refutation of anyone who might suppose otherwise because of the abundance of their afflictions in this world, He said: ﴿And indeed they are with Us, surely among the chosen and the excellent﴾. That is: according to the greatness and the knowledge that We possess. ﴿Among the chosen﴾: those who are most thoroughly purified, a purification so intense that it seems as though it were attained through effort. ﴿The excellent﴾: each one of whom is excellent to a high degree in goodness. Our afflicting them with calamities is evidence of this, not evidence of its opposite, as one whose heart has been obliterated supposes. This verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical figure in which two complementary elements are paired, one mentioned in each position while the other is left implied). The mention of "We purified them" (akhlasnāhum) first is evidence for "We chose them" (iṣṭafaynāhum) second, and the mention of "the chosen" (al-muṣṭafayn) is evidence for "the sincere" (al-mukhlaṣīn) first. The reason for this is that sincerity necessarily entails being chosen, especially when it is attributed to Him, whereas the reverse does not hold. The proof is His saying: ﴿Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those whom We chose from among Our servants; of them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fāṭir: 32].

When he had completed the account with the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham) and his son, peace be upon them both, who never departed from his care, and his grandson who was given good tidings of, so that they might be taken as examples in their patience in religion even when those who opposed them opposed them, he followed with his son whom he was commanded to be detached from. This was once by settling him near the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram), so that he would become a root in its own right in the most noble of places, and once by the command to sacrifice him in those noble sacred sites (al-mashaʿir al-karima). Thus the circumstances and actions attributed to him became among the great rites (manasik, the rites of pilgrimage), peace be upon him. He singled him out for mention to show that he is a great root in himself, among the roots of the leading imams.

So He said: ﴿And remember Ismaʿil﴾, that is, your father, and what he endured of trials through estrangement, solitude, loneliness, and facing death for the sake of God, more than once, and what came to him after that trial of relief, leadership, and remembrance in this town. ﴿And al-Yasaʿ﴾, that is, the one whom Ilyas, peace be upon him, appointed as his successor over the Children of Israel, and God gathered them to him after the severe opposition they had shown Ilyas, peace be upon him. ﴿And Dhu'l-Kifl﴾, that is, the one of great portion in fulfilment, through what he undertook (yakfuluhu) of every lofty matter and every pure righteous deed.

Since the description of those before Abraham, peace be upon him, with turning back (in repentance) had already been stated, and they were specified explicitly because of the preoccupations that distracted them from it, through both the trial of ease and the trial of hardship, and likewise through servitude (ʿubudiyyah) equally, and since the command to remember was, with the omission of the attribute for which they were mentioned and an allusion to it by hint, which does not prevent mentioning it, indicative of the utmost praise of him, because the mind goes off seeking it in every direction, He said, generalizing the description of servitude and turning back in it to all those mentioned, and joining, with what the conjunction indicates, a sentence that is not explicitly stated, according to its implied meaning: "Indeed they are those who turn back," so that it would serve as the justification for mentioning them with what He justified the mention of the first one mentioned among them:

﴿And all﴾, that is, of those mentioned in this surah among the prophets, are upholders of the due right of servitude; they are among Our good servants, from these three and those before them, ﴿are among the good ones﴾. That is, just as each of them is a turner-back (awwab) in the firmness of patience, as has passed in "al-Anbiyaʾ," and in other than that, in every good; and because patience comprises the whole path, they are the ones who must be followed in patience in religion and in holding fast to the way of the God-fearing.

When God, glory be to Him, had completed what He intended to say about those chosen servants, peace be upon them, who were saved by their patience and who saved those who called upon them, and whom He made a cause of success and not a cause of ruin, He said, affirming their nobility, the nobility of what they were mentioned for, urging the continual remembrance, contemplation, and reflection upon it in order to act by it, and explaining in detail what awaits them in the Hereafter for the deeds mentioned of them, and what awaits those who deviate from their path: ﴿This is a reminder﴾. That is, what We have recited to you of their affairs and the affairs of others. ﴿A reminder﴾, that is, an honor in this world and an admonition from the Qur'an, the Book full of reminder. Then He linked to His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who stray from the way of God will have a severe punishment﴾ [Sad: 26], what awaits their opposites, and He said, affirming, in response to those among the disbelievers of the Arabs (p-401) and others who deny this: ﴿And indeed﴾. It is permissible, and it is the better view, that this be conjoined to "this" (in ﴿This is a reminder﴾), and its implied sense would be: "This is a reminder for the patient, and for what their patience brought them to in this world, and that for them, in return for what We have granted them of righteous deeds, the sum of which is patience, is a good place of return." But He made apparent the attribute that led them to this destination, in order to generalize it to everyone who follows their example, urging them to follow. So He said: ﴿for the righteous﴾, that is, all the two groups in the attribute of God-consciousness, who, because of their God-consciousness, keep to the straight path; ﴿a good place of return﴾, that is, a destination and a place to which one returns.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 50:

When He, glory be to Him, had stirred desire for this reward, He substituted it for, or clarified it with, His saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾; that is, a dwelling in enduring pleasure, good living, flourishing, abundance, and nobility of origin.

Since "gardens" (jannat) is among the words that have become dominant as proper designations, He placed His saying ﴿opened﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of it; that is, opened up in great and thorough fashion, without them being made to suffer any weariness, exertion, or toil in opening them. The fact that this descriptor is given in the singular (mufattaḥatan) indicates that their being opened, despite their multiplicity, happens for them all at once, so that it is as if they were a single gate. ﴿For them﴾; that is, not for others; ﴿the gates﴾ which belong to them and which are within them. Thus they do not suffer the humiliation of chamberlains in entering them, nor the burden of seeking permission; the angels receive them with honor and esteem. (p-402)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 51:

When He had mentioned their dwelling (in Paradise) and the ease of their entry, He described their state at that time, saying: ﴿Reclining therein﴾; that is, they have no occupation other than delight, and no burden whatsoever is upon them. And since the one who reclines does not have his delight complete unless he is served, He indicated their nobility by His saying: ﴿calling therein﴾; that is, whenever they wish, without any hindrance at all, and without any need to stand or sit, which would require abandoning the reclining. And since their eating is only for enjoyment (tafakkuh), not for preserving the body from some harm, He said: ﴿for fruit, abundant﴾; so He named all their food "fruit" (fakihah). And since fruit is never tiresome, while drink is taken only in sufficient measure, He described the fruit separately from it, saying: ﴿and drink﴾.

Since eating and drinking lead to desire for women, especially with comfort, He said: ﴿And with them﴾, meaning: for them, without any separation at all. Since the context of favour conveys the abundance of what is granted, especially when it comes from the Great, He used the plural of paucity (jam' al-qilla) while intending abundance, because it is more well-known, clearer and more concise than "qawasir" (the plural shared by "qasir" and "qawsarra", pronounced with shadda and without it, for a container of dates). So He said: ﴿restraining (qasirat)﴾. Since they share one character in chastity and perfect beauty, He used the singular and said: ﴿of the glance﴾ (al-tarf), meaning the glance of them, for their chastity, and the glance of their husbands, for their beauty. Since the form of the plural of paucity does not diminish the meaning, as it occurs in the context of praise and favour, and since it is used metaphorically for abundance, He came in the pattern of the fawasil (rhymed endings) with His saying: ﴿equal in age (atrab)﴾, meaning: of one age with their husbands, which is youth. The companion was called "tirb" because dust touches his skin and his companion's skin at one time. Al-Baghawi said: "They are of thirty-three years of age, because that is more conducive to harmony, for mutual affection between peers is stronger and more lasting."

This is the commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 53:

When he had mentioned this bliss for the people of obedience, and had placed before it the punishment for the people of disobedience, He said: ﴿This is what you are promised﴾; that is, what has been mentioned here and what has passed; ﴿for the Day of Reckoning﴾ ... the verb being in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul) for brevity and to affirm that it is certain (tahattum): ﴿tu'adun﴾, from "al-wa'd" (promise) and "al-i'ad" (threat). The reading with the third person (al-ghayb) follows the form of the past tense; and whoever reads it in the second person (al-khitab) has turned the speech toward direct address for the sake of delight in the address, to energize their resolve and awaken their hearts. ﴿Li-yawm al-hisab﴾; that is, so that it may occur on that day.

Since this (state of affairs) could be thought to be one in which things exist and then come to an end, as is customary in the condition of the worldly life, He informed that it is on a different pattern from this, saying: ﴿Indeed, this﴾; that is, what is indicated by a pointing of one who is present and does not disappear; ﴿is truly Our provision﴾; that is, it is the provision which deserves to be attributed to Us in a manifestation of greatness. Therefore the outcome was: ﴿it has no cessation﴾; that is, no ending and no interruption. Rather, it is like water flowing continuously from its spring: whenever something is taken from it, it is replaced immediately, such that what is taken cannot be distinguished from what remains in any way. In this there is delight and bounty for the people of Paradise, through the abundance of what is with Him, and through witnessing what they used to believe and affirm about God (Exalted is He) regarding His power to restore at every moment, as a recompense in exact correspondence; the reverse of what comes upon the people of the Fire.

This is the commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 55:

When souls are inclined to desire and prone to perdition, they stand in need of greater warning and of severe terror. So (exalted is He) said, threatening those who abandon emulating these masters in the states of worship, and emphasizing what preceded of the promise to the disobedient and the warning to the stubborn rebels: ﴿This﴾; that is, this great matter, which is worthy of being placed before the eyes, namely that each of the two groups has what has been mentioned, even if the disbelievers deny it. The omission of the predicate (khabar), after its affirmation in the first part, is more terrifying, so that the imagination may go every way with it. ﴿And indeed for the transgressors﴾; that is, those who did not persevere in placing themselves in their proper stations by patience in what they were commanded, so they raised themselves above their rank, exceeded the limit, were haughty in disbelief in Him, were extravagant in sins and wrongdoing, became arrogant and proud, and thus were the most foolish of people. ﴿Surely an evil place of return﴾; that is, an evil destination and a place of return. (p-405) He substituted for it, or explained it, with his saying:

**Jahannam** (Hell): intensely blazing, encountering whoever enters it with utmost sternness and scowling.

Since their being assigned to it is not explicit about their punishment, he resumed with explicit statement of it in His saying: **﴿they will burn in it﴾**; i.e., they will enter it, and thus directly experience its severities. Since this conveyed the utmost aversion to it, and that for them there is no bed other than its embers, the sense is: "It will be a bed for them, encompassing them, so that its burning will cover them all," from which He stated as a consequence: **﴿So evil is the resting-place﴾**; i.e., the bed is it. For the purpose of a bed is the comfort of the body, whereas this melts skin and flesh; then it returns immediately, and whenever it melts, it returns, as a punishment for them, so that Allah shows them what they used to deny of renewal at every moment, perpetually and forever, just as they used to believe that perpetually and forever. A fitting recompense, the opposite of what the people of Paradise have of comfort and delight, by the renewal of everything of its fruit they had plucked and of its birds they had eaten, because they believe in renewal, so they attained this happiness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 57:

When he had mentioned that for the people of obedience there is fruit and drink, and what he described as the abode of the disobedient could only be punishment, and it was necessarily conveyed that the heat draws off from the people of the Fire an extract of pus and other things, he said: ﴿This﴾; i.e., the punishment is for the tyrants; ﴿so let them taste it﴾. Then he explained it with his saying: ﴿a boiling fluid﴾; i.e., hot water; and his use of the conjunction "wa" (and) indicates its firm establishment in each of the two attributes. So he said: ﴿and a dark, cold liquid﴾ (p. 406), i.e., a very great, extremely foul flow, cold, black, dark, intense in all these attributes, from pus and the like. It is, in the recitation of the majority (al-Jama'ah), with light pronunciation (al-takhfif), a noun, like "al-'adhab" (the punishment) and "al-nakal" (the exemplary chastisement), from "ghasaqat 'aynuhu" (his eye flowed), i.e., it flowed; and "ghasaqa al-shay'" (the thing became full), i.e., it filled up; and from it comes "al-ghasiq" (the darkening one), said of the moon, because of its fullness and completeness. In the recitation of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, with heavy pronunciation (al-tashdid), it is an adjective, like "al-khabbaz" (the baker) and "al-darrab" (the striker), indicating the intensity of its matter in all that it is applied to of flowing, cold, and blackness.

Now when there is in the Fire, may God save us from it by His pardon and mercy, an innumerable kind of punishment, He said, linking it (ʿāṭifan) to "this" (hādhā): ﴿And other⁠﻿—﻿﻿⁠ ... ﴾; that is, of the kinds of things tasted (madhūqāt). According to the reading of the people of Basra, it is in the plural to agree with "ukhrā," and "madhūq" is in the singular according to the reading of the others; and it is then for the genus (lil-jins). He informed about the subject (al-mubtada') with His saying: ﴿of its kind﴾; that is, the kind of this thing tasted (madhūq). And since what is intended is the multitude of those who are punished, namely the tyrants (al-ṭāghūn), and their punishment, along with its diversity in kinds, even though it is one in the genus of punishment, He stated them explicitly in His saying: ﴿pairs﴾; that is, they are (hum), or they are (hiya), or it is (huwa); meaning, the genus of their punishment comprises many kinds.

(p-407) Since the Book has made clear in this discourse that the tyrants who enter Hell are many kinds, and since it is customary that when kinds gather together there are exchanges of words, especially if they are among the arrogant and stubborn tyrants, the listener is moved to learn what that is. So He (exalted is He) said, resuming (*istinaf*, a new clause that answers an implied question) to answer it with what indicates their speaking with the most offensive kind of speech, which is mutual hostility arising from hatred and mutual aversion, the kind that naturally occurs among those who plotted a matter and it turned back upon them with ruin, in that each of them shifts the result that befell him onto his companion, and that is more severe for their punishment: ﴿This is a host rushing in with you﴾. That is, the most tyrannical of the tyrants says, when they first enter it, as they deserve, because they are misguided and misguide others, and they see a multitude of followers entering upon them: "This is a host," that is, a dense group, rushing on foot. And since they enter it with such force that the angels of punishment (*Zabāniyya*) push them, in the manner of one leaping, He said, using the singular form of the description to indicate that in their agreement in this and their rushing they are like a single soul: ﴿rushing in﴾, that is, one who throws himself into the hardship with sudden violence, without deliberation, being ﴿with you﴾.

Since the people of the Fire harm one another with groaning, wailing, crowding, pushing, weeping, lamentation, the pus and filth that flow from some of them onto others, and other kinds of distress, especially if they were followers of them in the world, and so they have come to be like them in that entry into the same rank, they do not refrain from pushing, quarreling, and contending with them. They said, as a resumed statement: ﴿No welcome for them﴾. Then they specified the one against whom the curse is directed, saying: ﴿for them﴾. This word is used in its most fitting place, because it indicates irritation and hatred, together with truthfulness regarding the one it refers to, which is the attachment of constriction. *Marhaban* is a noun of place (*maf'al*) from *al-rahb*, a mīmī verbal noun (one beginning with mīm), meaning spaciousness. That is: there is no spaciousness for them at all, these places have not been widened for them, nor these times, nor have they gained or possessed any ease. Therefore they justified their deserving of this curse by saying, emphasizing what had settled in their souls and what time had prolonged of their denial of it: ﴿They are indeed the burners of the Fire﴾. That is: whoever burns in it encounters a constriction that no one else encounters, and harms everyone who is near him.

When it was known, as is customary, that they would be affected by this statement, and that a longing would arise to learn what would become of them, whether the leaders would answer them or their awe of them, as it was in the world, would prevent them, (al-Biqa'i) informed them of what would indicate that the means (of help) had ceased there, so that none of them would fear another. So he said, resuming the account: ﴿They will say﴾; i.e., the followers, who are referred to as the group (fawj) because of their lowliness and the hiddenness of their affair; ﴿Rather, you﴾; i.e., exclusively; O leaders; ﴿No welcome﴾. They made clear by their words ﴿for you﴾; i.e., this which you called down upon us; you are more deserving of it than we are. Then they gave a reason for their statement, which conveyed that they had shared in the misguidance with them, and added to it by misguiding others. (p-409) So they said: ﴿You﴾; i.e., exclusively; ﴿brought it upon us﴾; i.e., the plunging into the punishment, by what you plunged us into of its causes, and what you presented in the abode of delusion of its adornment ﴿for us﴾. Since the plunging (iqtiham), which is a leaping or entering upon something swiftly, as if it were a leap, ends in settling, and both groups had settled in their seats in the Fire, they consequently said: ﴿Wretched is the abode﴾; i.e., your abode.

When the followers' words showed that they knew the cause of their misery was the leaders, and this necessarily brought the utmost of their rage against them, the listener became eager to know what would happen between them: would they be content with what they answered them, or would something else come from them? So he resumed the account, informing that they did not stop there, and knew that they could not take revenge on them: ﴿They will say﴾; i.e., the followers; ﴿Our Lord﴾; i.e., O You who are good to us, who prevented these from giving thanks to You; ﴿whoever brought this upon us﴾; i.e., the punishment, by the causes they brought upon us that thrust us into it. They put that first out of concern for it. They answered the conditional (shart, the "if" clause) with their words: ﴿then increase him﴾; i.e., in the punishment he deserves, by the measure that we deserve it ourselves, which is misguidance; ﴿double punishment﴾; i.e., in addition to that, its like once more, through misleading. They restricted it, seeking its magnitude, with their words, expressing it through the adverbial of place (zarf, a word indicating place or time) to convey the constraint in which the granted supplication had preceded (p-٤١٠) it, so that it would be another punishment. It is more eloquent than what is in al-A'raf, because the context here concerns the tyrants, whereas there it concerns disbelievers in general: ﴿in the Fire﴾; i.e., being in it. This is like the other verse, "Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great curse"; i.e., like our punishment twice over.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 62:

When he had mentioned their plunging into the punishment, and their mutual speech that indicated their disgrace, their regret, and their grief, he informed (the reader) of what indicates the increase of their loss, their regret, and their humiliation, by their knowledge of the salvation of the believers whom they used to mock and whom they used to demean. So he said: ﴿And they will say﴾; that is, the two groups, the leaders and the followers, after they had fulfilled their purpose, of which none of their disputing availed them anything: ﴿"What is (the matter) with us that we do not see﴾; that is, what has happened to us, preventing us from ﴿seeing﴾; that is, in the place into which we have been brought, ﴿men﴾; by which they mean the poor among the believers, ﴿whom we used to count﴾; that is, in the abode of this world, ﴿among the evil ones﴾; that is, the base people, who have no good in them, because they had cut the ties of kinship, divided the clan, corrupted relations among people, and altered the religion, by their constant opposing of people in their sayings and their deeds, along with what they were in of weakness, abasement, humiliation, and bad condition in this world.
