So the people of this world would think that their share of it was diminished, and that their many calamities in it were due to the badness of their state with God, and they did not realize that He (Exalted is He) protects His beloved ones from it, just as a person protects his sick one from food and drink; and whoever He wills good for, He afflicts him (with trials)."(p-٤١١)

Since they used to mock the believers and ridicule them, while they themselves were not deserving of this, and their state, in both their earnestness and their jesting, was far removed from it, they said, asking as a question (according to the reading of al-Haramayn, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim it is a definite question, *tahqiq*, while according to the readings of the others it is an assumed question, *taqdir*): ﴿Did we take them (as objects of mockery)?﴾ That is, we exerted ourselves and laboured in taking them. ﴿Sikhriyyan﴾ (for mockery): that is, we mocked them and ridiculed them, according to the reading with a kasra (*sikhriyyan*); or ﴿sukhriyyan﴾ with a damma, meaning we made them subservient, that is, we used them as servants. They were not worthy of that; rather they were better than us. They were not included here because of their lack of wickedness. It seems that they were more inclined to the supposition that they were in the Fire with them, but that they were prevented from seeing them. So they indicated this by the feminine form of the verb, relating the concealment of these people from them to a weakness in their sight, although their sight was at its strongest at that moment. Thus they said: ﴿Or have the eyes turned away from them?﴾ That is, have they swerved, passing beyond them?

Since He, exalted is He, will recreate creation on the Day of Resurrection with the utmost perfection in their bodies and their faculties, so that their sight will be the sharpest and most penetrating it can be: ﴿How well they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us﴾ [Maryam 19:38] and ﴿So your sight today is piercing﴾ [Qaf 50:22]. They counted their sight in this world, in comparison with that, as nothing. Therefore they defined their saying ﴿al-absar﴾ (the eyes) as meaning: of ours, the ones that, in reality, have no sight other than them. Thus we did not see them while they were among us and with us in the Fire, but some of its valleys, mountains and flames hid them from us. So ﴿am﴾ (or) is *mu'adilah* (equalising) to the clause of mockery. And by this estimation it becomes known that the meaning of the verse moves towards a true disjunction, whose meaning is: are they with us or not? So it is from *ihtibak* (a figure of speech in which one element is omitted from each of two parallel parts, the other being left to be inferred): it affirmed the taking mentioned, which necessarily entails, by the rule of contradiction between the two clauses, that those mocked were not with them in the Fire at first, as a proof of its opposite, which is that they were with them in it. And it affirmed the swerving of the eyes second, which entails in the same manner that they were with them in the Fire, as a proof of its opposite first, which is that they were not with them. The secret of this is that the position calls for their regret, and their blaming themselves for their error, and what is mentioned of them is more fitting for that.

When this was a matter of great awe, a warning to whoever has intellect and reflects on it while free of his own desires, and when good fortune (al-judud) kept people from believing it, it became a place for emphasizing the report about it. So He said: ﴿Indeed, that is true﴾, meaning the great matter previously reported, ﴿is true﴾, meaning established, with no escape from its occurrence. When its content occurs, this report about it corresponds to what actually happens.

Since the hardest and most painful part of it for them was ﴿the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾, He made that alone the thing reported. He said, explaining it and reporting about a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence) in a resumptive construction (istinaf, a new sentence that begins anew), whose estimated form is "he is": ﴿the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾. This is because what the Fire brings them is nothing but evil and misery, so it is called "dispute." (p-٤١٣)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 65:

Since it has been their habit, when being warned, to say: "Hasten for us this [punishment], if you are truthful in what you claim" — and it is certain that none can bring this about except God (al-Ilah) — they became as though they had attributed to him the claim of divinity. (The Exalted) said, alerting to this and commanding him to answer: ﴿Say﴾; that is, to the one who says this to you: ﴿I am only a warner﴾; that is, one who frightens those who disobey; and I have not claimed that I am a god, so that this should be demanded of me, for none can do the like of this except God. So this is a restriction of the attribute to the one described (qasr qalb), correcting a false attribution to him. He used the singular of the restricted attribute in his saying ﴿and there is not﴾; and he intensified the negation with his saying ﴿any god﴾; that is, any worshipped one in truth, because He encompasses all the attributes of perfection. Since the context concerns tawhid, which is the foundation of the religion (usul al-din), he turned the speech from the locus of greatness to something greater and clearer, so he said: ﴿except God﴾. For comprehensiveness he expressed it with the proper name (ism 'alam), which gathers all the Most Beautiful Names; and if anything shared with Him, it would not be all-encompassing. For uniqueness, to furnish proof of this, he said: ﴿the One﴾; that is, in every respect, so it is impossible that He should have a part, or that He should have a like, for then He would be needy and equal. ﴿the Subduer﴾; that is, the One who overpowers others to do what He wills. This is a proof that He alone is God, and that their gods are far from deserving divinity, because they are many, equal in resemblance, and in need.

Rabb al-samawat (the Lord of the heavens) — that is, their Originator; their Preserver, in their height, their vastness, their solid making, along with what they possess of adornment and benefits. He used the plural (samawat) because the context is one of power, and establishing the proof of their multiplicity is easy. [Lord of] the earth as well, in its vastness, its massiveness, its density, and the wonders within it.

Since the speaker is free to choose, as Ibn Malik said in al-Kafiya al-Shafiya, when rational beings mix with non-rational ones, in using whichever he wishes of "man" (man), which is mostly used for rational beings, and "ma" (ma), which is the opposite; and since it might occur to someone that His (exalted be He) power over rational beings is different from His power over others, because of the stratagems they possess by which they guard against what is feared and consider the outcomes of affairs, He indicated that His rule over them is like His rule over others, without distinction, by expressing them with "ma," whose original and most common usage is for what does not reason. The context of greatness, with oneness and its effects, necessarily indicates their inclusion in worship. So He said: ﴿and what is between them﴾ — that is, between the two horizons: the space, the air, and other elements, plants, animals, rational and otherwise. He nurtures each of these by bringing into existence and sustaining it as He wills, even if that which is nurtured dislikes it. This indicates His dominance and His sole authority over all His affairs.

Since the context is one of warning, He repeated what indicates dominance, saying: ﴿the Almighty (al-'Aziz)﴾ — that is, the One who is difficult to reach, who overcomes everything, and whom nothing overcomes. Since it is established that He overcomes everything and nothing overcomes Him, and since the indication of these two great attributes toward threat is more evident than their suggestion of promise, this was the place for their saying: "Why does He not hasten destruction upon those who oppose Him?" So He said: ﴿the Oft-Forgiving (al-Ghaffar)﴾ — that is, the One who repeatedly covers over whatever sins He wills, out of forbearance until a time; the One who erases them completely with respect to whichever of His servants He wills, as He did with most of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), for He forgave them what they had committed before Islam.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 67:

Since by this His oneness and His power were established, and yet that did not restrain them from their misguidance, nor turn them back from their arrogance and their obstinacy, even though it necessitates that every person turn toward Him and never turn away from Him, He said, commanding him (ﷺ) with what would alert them to the magnitude of their error: ﴿Say, "It is a great news,"﴾ — that is, this matter which I have recited to you, of reports about the past and the future, of the Resurrection containing the aforementioned dispute, and other things, and of rulings and admonitions. By its content, oneness is established, and by its inimitability it is verified that it is the speech of Allah, together with the established oneness, the perfection of power, and all attributes of perfection: ﴿a great news﴾ — that is, a report that exceeds description in majesty and greatness, by the indication of its expression and its attributes. Only a heedless person, who has no awareness and no sound judgment, turns away from the like of it.

Since they claimed that they were the greatest of people in their attention to strange matters and in their searching after the subtle and the sublime virtues, he rebuked them by saying, describing it: ﴿You are from it﴾; that is, specifically, not from anything else, while the situation is that everything else is among the trivial matters. And since most of them were prepared for Islam and for returning from disbelief, he did not say "turning their backs" (mudbirun) nor "turning away" (tu'ridun), but rather said: ﴿turning away (mu'ridun)﴾; that is, turning away is established for you at this time. Yet it was fitting for you to devote yourselves to it specifically and to turn away from everything other than it, because in that lies complete happiness. Had you turned to it with contemplation, you would have known with certainty my truthfulness, and that I do not desire for you anything but happiness in this world and the Hereafter; so you would have hastened to turn to me and to accept what I say.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 69:

When He restricted his noble self to warning, and they were disputing with him and attributing lying to him, He indicated his truthfulness and the great magnitude of this news by His saying: ﴿I had no knowledge﴾; and He intensified the negation through emphasis in His saying: ﴿of the Highest Assembly﴾ (i.e., "from the side of anyone among the people"), as you know this from my condition. He has no comprehensive knowledge whatsoever of ﴿the Highest Assembly﴾, i.e., the group characterized by nobility, ﴿the Highest﴾; and they are the angels, the people of the lofty heavens, and Adam and Iblis. It seems that God's address to them was through an angel, as is most fitting for His majesty and glory. Thus it is sound that the dispute was between the assembly ﴿when﴾, i.e., at the time when, ﴿they were disputing﴾. And since He used the singular for the description of the assembly, signifying that they are in agreement in the loftiness of the rank of obedience as if they were one thing, He used the plural lest the reality of unity be supposed; so He said: ﴿they were disputing﴾, i.e., concerning the matter of Adam, peace be upon him, the first vicegerent on earth; (p-417) rather, the absolute vicegerent, since the vicegerency of his offspring derives from his vicegerency; and concerning the expiations that occur among them. Likewise, I had no knowledge of the people of the Fire when they dispute, nor of the adversaries who entered upon Dawud, peace be upon him, whom God (Exalted) made a vicegerent on earth, when they disputed. I know this with knowledge that conforms to the truth, by the testimony of the earlier scriptures; and you know that I never mixed with any scholar at all. So this is one of the signs of prophethood, clearly showing that I did not know this except through revelation, because I am the Messenger of God. Here he expressed it in the present tense, although it occurred and passed from the beginning of time, as a reminder of that state and an informing of what they are now in, of the like of it in the ranks, as will come shortly in the sacred hadith. And regarding the disputing of the people of the Fire, which has not yet taken place, he expressed it in the past tense, as an alert that its occurrence is beyond doubt, so it is as though it has occurred and been completed, because the One whose decree cannot be reversed has finished His decree; because He is the One, so there is no partner for Him, and no contender.

When they might say, in their obstinacy: "Perhaps he is only like [one to whom] what he did not know was revealed by knowledge, [or one to whom] power over what he was not able to do is revealed, so that he hastens death for us, then resurrection, so that we see the disputing [of the people of the Fire] that you told us of, depicted, perhaps we will believe you in what you brought." He said, answering them, restricting the revelation to its restriction to warning, which is conveying what was sent down to him, and not the hastening of anything of what they were threatened with: ﴿Say﴾; that is, ﴿it is﴾; that is, "only," ﴿revealed﴾; that is, at any time, and he made it passive because that is sufficient to alert them to the point of indication, that his claim is only to prophethood (al-nubuwwah) and not to divinity (al-ilahiyyah); ﴿to me, that﴾. Since the revelation is speech, Abu Ja'far read with a kasra on ﴿that I am only a warner﴾; that is, my restriction to warning, not that I bring about what God threatens. So "anna-ma" (that only) is the object of "yuhā" (is revealed), the substitute for the subject in both readings (al-qa'im maqam al-fa'il). Although the two grammatical analyses differ, the estimate on the reading of the majority (with the fatha) is: "except the warning," or "except my being a warner"; and on the reading with the kasra: "except this statement, which is that I say to you such and such." ﴿Clear﴾; that is, I leave no ambiguity in what I convey, in any respect.

When He showed that he (the Prophet) is a warner, and removed what they might have raised against him, He followed it with the time of the dispute of the Exalted Assembly, or as a replacement for the first "idh" ("when"). So He said: ﴿When﴾, i.e., at the time when ﴿He said﴾. This shows that all of this is a kindness toward him and a blessing upon him, by mentioning the attribute that indicates it. He turned the speech from the first person to the second person, because that is more firmly rooted in praise and more indicative that it is the Word of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Say: "Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel..."﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:97]. This is a proof that might give the impression that it is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) governing "yuḥā" (is revealed) or "nadhīr" (warner). So He said: ﴿Your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is good to you by making you the best of creation and the most honoured of them before Him, for He has given you al-Kawthar, which is everything you could need. ﴿to the angels﴾, and they are the Exalted Assembly, and Iblis was among them, because he was then with them and counted among them. Since they knew, by a proof from God that had been shown to them, as mentioned earlier in Surah al-Baqarah, that humankind would commit corruption, they found it far-fetched that He, glory be to Him, would create one in whom there is corruption, because He is the Wise, and there is no wise one besides Him. So He, glory be to Him, emphasised His statement to them: ﴿Indeed I am creating a human being (basharan)﴾, i.e., a person whose skin is visible, not covered by feathers, hair, or anything else. The emphasis is meant as a proof of what had passed of their dispute with God (exalted is He), which He indicated by the word "dispute." He explained its origin by His saying, linked to "creating" or to the description of "basharan": ﴿from clay﴾. "I will make him My vicegerent on earth, even though there is corruption in that, because I want to manifest My forbearance, My mercy, My pardon, and other of My attributes which would not be fitting in wisdom to manifest except along with sins." Based on the hadith: "Had you not sinned and then sought forgiveness, Allah would have brought forth a people who sin and then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them." Al-Qushayri said: His informing the angels of this indicates the magnification of the status of Adam (peace be upon him), because He created what He created of the two worlds, the Garden, the Fire, the Throne, the Chair, and the angels, and He did not say about any of them what He said about the description of Adam (peace be upon him) and his offspring, and He did not command prostration to anything other than him.

When He, glory be to Him, informed them of what He intended to do, He made the following statement its consequence: ﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾; that is, when I have prepared him by completing his creation for what is intended from him, namely the acceptance of the soul and what follows from it; ﴿and breathed into him of My Spirit﴾; so he became sentient and breathing. He, glory be to Him, likened His bestowing of the soul to what results from a human's blowing: the flame of fires and other forms of moving, calming, increasing and decreasing; and He attributed it to Himself, glory be to Him, as an honouring of him. (p-420) ﴿Then fall down before him﴾; that is, specifically; ﴿in prostration﴾; that is, prostrate to him, out of honour, in compliance with My command; a prostration that is of the utmost obedience, choice and love, as though you had fallen down without choice. So they did what He, glory be to Him, commanded them, without hesitation. For this reason He mentioned their action, although its feminine form was permissible; so He said:

"So the angels prostrated" — that is, when He breathed into him of the spirit; ﴿the angels﴾, as Allah had commanded them. Since ascribing the report to all of them might be intended to mean most of them, he emphasized it with his saying ﴿all of them﴾, desiring to remove the metaphorical sense.

Since one or a few of them, who are of no account due to weakness or the like, might not detract from this, he removed that possibility with his saying ﴿every one of them﴾, while also conveying that the prostration occurred at one and the same moment, to inform of the intensity of their submission, the excellence of their readiness for obedience, and their preparedness.

Then he added further clarification to the generality through the exception, which is its criterion, saying: ﴿Except Iblis﴾. He referred to him by this name because it derives from iblas (إبلاس), which means the cutting off of hope, indicating that at the very beginning of God's address to him, with rebuke against him, it was in a manner from which the perpetuity of wrath upon him and the certainty of punishment for him became known.

And since the exception made known that he did not prostrate, and since the framework of the surah rests on the arrogance of the disbelievers, in that they are in pride and opposition, he explained that what prevented him from prostrating was (p-421) pride, as a warning against it, limiting himself in explaining the dispute to it and to what is connected with it, saying: ﴿he was arrogant﴾; that is, he sought to be greater than being commanded to prostrate to him, and he brought pride into being against God's command. He was one of those who were deeply rooted in this description of arrogance, just as you disbelievers have been arrogant toward Our messenger. We will also raise Our messenger ﷺ, just as We raised Adam, Our chosen one (peace be upon him), above those who were arrogant toward prostrating to him, and We will make him a khalifah (vicegerent) of this existence, just as We made Adam (peace be upon him) one. This was indicated in this surah by opening it with a khalifah and closing it with a khalifah. The Messenger of God ﷺ was commanded to mention the circumstances of each of the two.

Since the past-tense verb may give the impression that a description came about in him which had not existed before, and since the intended meaning was: "so he disbelieved by that," he joined to it, as an explanation that he was created with disbelief and that nothing arose from him except the manifestation of that to creation, the words ﴿and he was﴾; that is, by nature and disposition; ﴿among the disbelievers﴾; that is, deeply rooted in the description of disbelief, which originates in pride toward the truth, and which necessarily entails humiliation before falsehood. Thus the verse is of the type called ihtibak (interlocking): he mentioned the act of arrogance first, as an indication of the act of disbelief second, and the description of disbelief second, as an indication of the description of arrogance first. The secret of this is that what he mentioned is more effective in warning that whoever has pride in him is led by it to disbelief.

Since the king's command was one that its violator deserved to have a command issued against him, one that would be used to take vengeance on him, the listener became eager to know what the king had said to him. So he resumed the explanation with His words: ﴿He said﴾. He showed that Iblis was in a place of distance by saying: ﴿O﴾. He showed his despair of (p-422) mercy and that he had no answer at all by expressing him as: ﴿Iblis, what﴾, that is, what thing, ﴿prevented you from prostrating﴾. He showed what obliges obedience to Him, even had He commanded the veneration of something that does not reason, by saying, using the particle for non-rational beings for one who, at the time of prostration to him, was rational and of complete intellect: ﴿to that which I created﴾. So I am the one who knows it, and what it deserves, and no one else does. I did not command prostration to it except for a wisdom in the command and as a trial for others. He confirmed the explanation of this by mentioning the hand and its dual form, so He said: ﴿with My two hands﴾, that is, without the mediation of any cause among the kinds of this sort. This is only for greater distinction. The intended meaning of "hand" here is a noble attribute, other than blessing and power, known to Him, glorified is He. Those who are deeply versed in the two sciences of the language and the Sunnah (linguistics and prophetic tradition) hold that He specially assigned it to the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, to honor him. In the dual form of "hand" there is an indication that it may have manifested in it the meanings of the left, though each of his two hands is blessed.

Then He divided the obstacle into seeking exaltation and possessing exaltation, with denunciation of him for relying on either of these two, so He said, in the form of an interrogative of affirmation together with denial and rebuke, as a clarification that it necessarily follows for him, beyond what he disbelieved in, that he be in one of these two matters: ﴿Are you arrogant?﴾, that is, did you seek to be higher than him while you know that you are below him? Thereby you are a wrongdoer, and so you were among the arrogant, those deeply rooted in the description of wrongdoing, for whoever dares against the lowest of it is close to reaching its highest. ﴿Or were you﴾, that is, by what you have of firmly established disposition, ﴿of the exalted﴾, that is, the great ones who deserve greatness, while I do not know that about you, so I would have diminished you from your rank. Then you were unjust in My command to you by what I commanded you, and therefore you exalted yourself and did not prostrate to him. This is the intended meaning, not what some of the heretics (al-malahida) say, that the exalted were a group of angels who did not prostrate because they were not commanded. That is because it would be a defect in the emphasized generality with this great emphasis, and against the interpretation of the scholars of it without any doubt.

The verse is of ihtibak (a device in which two parts are left implicit, each being indicated by the other): the verb of arrogance first indicates the verb of exaltation second, and the description of exaltation second indicates the description of arrogance first. The secret of this is that denying the unrestricted act entails denying the restricted one, because the unrestricted is the restricted with an addition; and denying the description entails denying the act, because it is part of it. Moreover, denying the act in this sense entails denying the act in that sense, so each of the two acts is indicated as denied twice: once by denying the act equivalent to it, and once by denying its own description. The two descriptions are likewise. The act of pride is more worthy of denial than the act of exaltation.

And "am" (أم) is equivalent to the interrogative hamzah, though some of them omitted it in their recitation, since "am" indicates it. Even if the verb differs. Abu Hayyan said: Sibawayh said: you say, "Did you strike Zayd or did you kill him?" Beginning here with the verb is better, because you are only asking about one of the two, not knowing which of them occurred, and you are not asking about the place of one of them, as if you said, "Which of these occurred?" End.

(p-424) When He, glorified is He, cut him off with this denial, He indicated his silencing through His words, in a resumptive construction: ﴿He said﴾, claiming that he was of the exalted ones: ﴿"I am better than him."﴾ That is: there is no wisdom in commanding me to prostrate to him. Then he explained what he claimed with his words: ﴿"You created me from fire"﴾, that is, while it is at the utmost of strength and brightness; ﴿"and You created him from clay"﴾, that is, while it is at the utmost of density and weakness.

The continuation of the explanation of what had aroused expectation regarding the knowledge of its answer was taken up again, with His words, turning away from criticizing his answer because its invalidity is evident, [namely] that the created, the one who is nurtured, has no objection whatsoever against his Lord: ﴿He said: "Then get out of it"﴾; that is, because of your arrogance, and your attributing to the Wise One, against whom there is no objection, injustice; ﴿from it﴾; that is, from the Garden, the place of purity from outward and inward ailments. Then He gave the reason for that with His words, emphasizing it for the sake of the claim that he deserved the closest nearness: ﴿for indeed you are accursed﴾; that is, deserving of expulsion and stoning (rajm), which is casting with stones, and it is for the sake of intensifying the expulsion.

When the expulsion may occur in a short time, he clarified that it is lasting, by his saying, emphasizing (with the emphatic particle), as an indication of informing about what is in his own self of increased pride: ﴿And indeed upon you﴾; that is, specifically. And since the context here is speech in a place other than the manifestation of greatness, he did not bring the lam of speech (lam al-kalam); unlike in "al-Hijr"; so he said: ﴿My curse﴾; that is, my removal (from mercy), along with expulsion, disgrace, humiliation, and abasement, dominating that over you permanently, overpowering you, such that you cannot be released from it in any way. As for others than you, they are not specifically destined for cursing; rather, they remain between hope and fear. No created being has knowledge that he is certainly cursed while he is alive, except one whom a prophet of the prophets has informed about that. Then he limited this curse by his saying: ﴿until the Day of Religion﴾; that is, when that day comes, He begins the recompense of every doer for what he did; and no time remains for a wrongdoer in which he may make up what he missed. At that point, all those deserving the curse become known, and the knowledge of that is no longer specific to Iblis; rather, knowledge encompasses all the people of the curse. So the end point (ghayah) relates to the knowledge of the specificity of the curse, not to the curse itself.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 79:

When this had occurred, the listener became eager to know what Iblis had said in response. So Allah, glorified is He, informed of it in a context that makes clear that He withheld from him success (tawfiq), so he did not ask for relief, nor did he turn toward repentance. Rather, abandonment (khidhlan) overtook him through persistence in rebellion (tughyan), so he sought that which would increase him in curse (la'nah) through misguidance (al-idlal) and utter immersion in error (al-i'raq fi al-dalal), the opposite of what He had bestowed upon Adam, peace be upon him. So he said, mentioning the attribute of beneficence and the cause for requesting respite, because of what the apparent wording had emboldened him with regarding the matter that the curse is limited by the Day of Religion:

﴿He said: "My Lord,"﴾; that is, O You who have done good to me by bringing me into existence and placing me among the noble angels; ﴿"then give me respite"﴾; that is, because of what You have afflicted me with of expulsion; ﴿"until the day they are raised."﴾; that is, Adam and his offspring, whom You will raise by the resurrection of all creation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 80:

﴿قالَ﴾; emphasizing, because the like of that, in breaking the customary order (al-'adah), is hardly conceivable; ﴿فَإنَّكَ﴾; that is, because of this request; ﴿مِنَ المُنْظَرِينَ﴾ [He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite."]; and this indicates that such respite is also granted to others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 81:

When he had embellished his expression with what implies the request that he not die, for the Day of Resurrection is a time for the outpouring of life, not for its ebbing, and for its expansion, not its contraction, He prevented him from that by saying: ﴿Until the Day of the time appointed﴾. And since his embellishment in the request had shown his ignorance of what He is most knowledgeable of, namely the inevitability of death for everyone who is not in the abode of eternity, a matter which Allah (Exalted is He) made abundantly clear in informing about it, He said: ﴿the appointed time﴾; and it is the First Blast and what follows it.

When this response was a cause for him to humble himself and turn back in gratitude for it, and for him to transgress, rebel and be ruined, because it is an empowerment and a preparation for evil, the listener became eager to know what would come of these two causes. He clarified that al-Khidhlan (divine abandonment, the withholding of help) prevented him from choosing goodness, by His saying: ﴿He said: "Then by Your might"﴾; i.e., the might which refuses that anything should happen to anyone other than in accordance with it. It is also permissible that the bā' (الباء) be for the oath (al-qasam): ﴿I will surely mislead them﴾; i.e., the descendants of Adam (peace be upon him); ﴿all together﴾. Al-Qushayri said: If he had known His might, he would not have (p-427) sworn by it to oppose Him.

When the One who is Able (al-Qadir) had knowledge that He had not created Adam (peace be upon him) and honored him with what He honored him with in order to make all his descendants wretched, [Iblis] said: ﴿except Your servants﴾. He attributed them to Himself (Glorified is He), as a reminder that others had stripped themselves of the honor of servitude to Him, in relation to those who obeyed Him. Since it was possible that the exception would refer to non-humans, he restricted it by His words: ﴿among them the sincere ones﴾; that is, those whom Allah (Exalted is He) purified for His obedience, so they sincerely directed their intention toward it. And it is understood from the exception that they are few, and that the misguided are the norm.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 84:

When the anticipation of its answer had arisen, he indicated it by his saying: ﴿He said: "Then the truth"﴾; that is, "Then, because of your misleading [them], and their being led astray, I say the truth"; ﴿and the truth﴾; that is, nothing else, ever; ﴿I say﴾; that is, I say nothing but the truth. For everything I have said is established, so no one can overturn it or diminish it. And since his being granted respite might perhaps have been a cause for his hope of escape, He cut off his hope by what He brought forth in the style of emphasis, in his saying, as a response to an implied oath and as a clarification of the truth. And in the reading of ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah, with the nominative "al-ḥaqq" (fa-al-ḥaqqu), the truth itself is the one sworn by; that is, "Then the truth is My oath." And the answer [is]:

[p. 428] ﴿Surely I will fill﴾; what lies between is a parenthetical clause making clear that this is something that can never be broken at all. ﴿Hell﴾: that is, the great Fire, whose nature is to scowl upon whoever is sentenced to enter it. ﴿with you﴾: that is, yourself, and everyone who is of your kind, of your nature, from among all the jinn. ﴿and with whoever﴾: since the predominant tenor of this surah's contexts is a good end, the singular pronoun in "tabi'a" (follows) is the more fitting, so that the judgment is understood as applying to each individual, and then to the group as a whole. He therefore said ﴿follows you﴾. Since a captious objector might say, "Those who fill Hell are perhaps not human," He said ﴿from among them﴾: that is, from among the people for whose sake you asked for respite. He emphasized the pronoun in "minka" (with you) and the relative in "mimman" (with whoever) with His words ﴿all of them﴾, meaning there is no difference in this between any one of you. This dispute, which He (glorified is He) made clear had taken place among the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la), became the occasion for them to uncover many sciences, among them that prostration, greetings, seeking forgiveness, and expiations are the means of reaching Allah, and of drawing near to Him. Thereafter they came to dispute about these matters. This affair thus became the occasion for the Prophet (ﷺ) to be informed of the secrets of the dominion (al-mulk) and the realm of the unseen (al-malakut). To this the hadith narrated by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who said "hasan gharib" (sound, strange), al-Darimi, and al-Baghawi in his Tafsir points, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I became drowsy and fell into a deep sleep, and then my Lord came to me, in another narration: a messenger from my Lord, in the best of forms, and said to me: 'O Muhammad.' I said: 'Here I am, my Lord, at Your service and bidding.' He said: 'Do you know what the Exalted Assembly is disputing about?' I said: 'No, my Lord,' in another narration: 'I said: You know best, O my Lord,' twice. He said: He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coolness between my breasts, or he said: my chest, and so I knew what is in the heavens and what is in the earth." In another narration: "what is between the east and the west." In the narration of al-Darimi and al-Baghawi: "Then he recited this verse: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. He said: 'O Muhammad, do you know what the Exalted Assembly is disputing about?' I said: 'Yes, concerning the degrees and the expiations.' He said: 'And what are they?' I said: 'Remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, performing ablution thoroughly in hardship' — in another narration: 'in the sabarat' (bitter cold) — 'and waiting for one prayer after another.' He said: 'Whoever does that lives in goodness, dies in goodness, and is from his sin as on the day his mother bore him.' Then He said: 'O Muhammad.' I said: 'Here I am, at Your service and bidding.' He said: 'When you pray, say: O Allah, I ask You to do good deeds, to abandon evil deeds, to love the poor, that You forgive me and have mercy on me, and when You intend a trial for Your servants, take me to You without being tried.' He said: 'The degrees are: spreading the greeting of peace, feeding the food, and praying at night while people are asleep.'" Al-Mundhiri said: al-Mala' al-A'la are the closest angels; and "al-sabarat," with an unpointed sin (s) and a sakin ba', is the plural of "sabra," which means intense cold. Our shaykh, in his takhrij of the Hadiths of al-Firdaws, attributed it to Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi on the authority of Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him) also; and he said: "There is also in this chapter a narration from Thawban (may Allah be pleased with him) in Ahmad ibn Mani', and from Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Rafi', Abu Umamah, Abu 'Ubaydah, Usamah, Jabir ibn Samurah, Jubayr ibn Mut'im, Usamah ibn 'Umayr, and Anas (may Allah be pleased with them all) in Ahmad." This, then, is a dispute whose details, once known, caused the first dispute, namely the one concerning Adam (peace be upon him) and his descendants. The knowledge bestowed upon Muhammad (ﷺ) through asking about this dispute is like the knowledge bestowed upon his father Adam (peace be upon him) through that dispute. This dispute, and Allah knows best, is their disagreement about the measures of the reward of those who act, the reward alluded to by "degrees," which reason motivates, reason that calls to the best constitution (ahsan taqwim); and the punishment alluded to by "expiations," whose causes are called for by satanic whisperings that return one to the lowest of the low, the respite for which Iblis asked. The cause of their disagreement [p. 431] over the measures of the reward is the difference in the measures of inward deeds: the soundness of intentions, the strength of resolve, the intensity of striving and its softness, according to the impulses of desires and appetites. The knowledge of these things was the cause of their knowing them through the dispute over the affair of Adam (peace be upon him) and what resulted from it, detailed by subtle matters, which show that virtue does not lie in outward matters, but in what Allah bestows of inward matters. Their speculation about this was called a dispute, to indicate the greatness of what they speculated about, since dispute arises only over a precious matter. The meaning is that each of the angels is occupied with the service assigned to him, so there is no contention among them carried on with utmost seriousness and eagerness, as is the nature of dispute, except in this case, because of their great wonder at it, knowing how difficult these matters are for a human being, given the distractions and diversions he has from them, through the knowledge Allah granted them as a reward for their submission to obedience by prostrating after that dispute. Thus a human's turning away from his diversions and appetites toward what the angels have in ranks of obedience, and turning away altogether from disobedience, is an extreme wonder. His (ﷺ) knowledge of what is in the heavens and what is in the earth is general knowledge, for at the time of the vision the dominion of both was made manifest to him. The attribution of all this to the knowledge of Allah (exalted is He) is like the comparison mentioned by al-Khidr to Musa (peace be upon them both) regarding the sparrow's drop from the sea. What the scholars have said about this is that it is an approximation for understanding, for in reality there is no comparison between the knowledge of anyone and His knowledge (exalted is He), nor does His knowledge ever diminish, in any way that would bring deficiency or weakness, (glorified is He): ﴿Say: If the sea were ink﴾ [al-Kahf: 109]; ﴿and if whatever trees are in the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27]; ﴿On the day Allah will gather the messengers and say: What was your answer? They will say: We have no knowledge﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. It is said to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning people who were driven away from his Basin: "You do not know what they innovated after you," and he says: "Away with them, away!"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 86:

When he had completed what he intended as proof that what he had brought them is a great news, from which they turn away, by what he reported of the unseen, together with the inimitability (i'jaz) that it possesses, and thereby it became established what required that he is truthful in his attribution to Allah (Exalted), and he concluded with a warning against following Iblis, he commanded him to disown his path, and to negate from himself what might lead to the charge of fabricating, by his saying: ﴿Say﴾; that is, to your community; ﴿I do not ask you﴾; a request of seeking elevation; and he attached to it, not to "wage" (ajr), his saying: ﴿for it﴾; that is, for the conveying and the warning, concerning what you are exposed to of destruction through turning away. So the particle of elevation (isti'la') is for guarding against asking for affection in kinship (al-mawaddah fi al-qurba) and good following, for these two are things asked for, and they are the spirit of the religion. But their request is not elevated over the conveying, such that if they were absent, it would be absent. And he intensified the negation by his saying: ﴿any wage﴾; that is, so that there would be no doubt for you in rejecting it. ﴿And I am not of those who affect (al-mutakalliffin)﴾; that is, those who adorn themselves with what is not of their people, of speech or of deed, who burden themselves with forging speech and affecting it, and arranging it in some manner, by verse, or prose rhymed (saj'), or sermons, or other than that, or placing themselves in other than their proper places, as Iblis did. I am not of them in any way, nor am I counted among them; I do not do their deeds, nor do I love them, nor do I partisan for them. So it is more eloquent than "and I am not one who affects," for you have known me throughout my life to be thus. And it is known that if that were in my nature, I would not have refrained from it throughout the period of my growth, of childhood and youth, the two periods in which natural dispositions are found and are not found after them. So when it is established that that was not in me at that time, it is established that it is impossible after it, because it is settled that no natural disposition exists after ceasing to grow, at the age of forty-three. So when it is known that I am not like that, it is known that I am commanded to what I am engaged in of speech and deed, and so I am of those who are charged (al-mukallafin), not those who affect (al-mutakalliffin). Thus everyone who says or does what he has not been commanded to is an affecter (mutakalliff). And al-Tha'labi narrated, with his chain, from the hadith of Salamah ibn Nufayl (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Prophet (ﷺ); and al-Bayhaqi, in Shu'ab al-Iman, from the saying of Ali ibn Arta'ah; and Abu Nu'aym, in al-Hilyah, from the saying of Wahb: "The sign of the affecter is three: he contends with one above him, he reaches for what cannot be attained, and he says what he does not know."

Since He had established the factors that necessitate that it comes from Allah, and had removed the impediments, He explained its true nature, which does not go beyond what they attributed to it, by His saying: ﴿It is not﴾, that is, it is nothing other than, ﴿but a reminder﴾, that is, an admonition and an honour, ﴿to the worlds﴾, that is, to all of them. Each individual understands what his faculties can bear, whether he is intelligent or dull, in accordance with the sublimity it possesses, to which no speech comes close, unlike poetry and soothsaying (kahanah), whose focus is rhymed prose (saj') and lying in reporting some of the unseen matters. For these two, despite the lowliness of their rank, are understood only by a few of the worlds, and only that (level of understanding) and that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 38, verse 88:

Since the implied sense was, "I know that," he joined to it his statement, as an answer to an oath: ﴿And you will surely know its news﴾; that is, you too; ﴿its news﴾; that is, the truth of my words in everything I have informed you of in it (the Qur'an) and about it (the Qur'an), of the great reports; and in what is indicated by the opening of these prophets mentioned in this surah with "a khalifah" (vicegerent) and their closing with "a khalifah": that your might will turn to humiliation, your discord will turn to conciliation and harmony, and your large numbers will turn to paucity; and that what I am engaged in now will lead me to the vicegerency of God on His earth; and that the middle of my affair will turn to the like of the vicegerency of the first (Adam) over the whole Arabian Peninsula, which is the land of the Great Mosque, which is before the Farthest Mosque, which is the place of His vicegerency; then the affair of my vicegerency will be extended throughout the rest of the lands, and it will continue until it covers the earth in its length and breadth, at the hand of his son Jesus, peace be upon him, the seal of the greatest of my followers, my helpers, and my partisans.

He omitted the preposition to indicate that knowledge encompasses the time of the aftermath, and so said: ﴿after a while﴾; that is, unspecified to you, known to me, in this world when my servants prevail over you, and in the Hereafter absolutely. They were delayed until this time only so that the proof against them might be complete, their arguments would be cut off, and the sins for which they deserve punishment would reach their limit. Indeed, by God, they knew that, and then they regretted it, those who died among them and those who lived, before twenty years had passed since the exaltation of His word, the manifestation of His message, and the completion of His religion. Knowledge remained for them and for those after them through what He spread in it of sciences and what He gathered in it of noble traces, and what was promised in it of the past was manifested up to this time and until every perishing thing perishes, and then they are resurrected to Paradise or the Fire. This verse has thus established, from the Qur'an's being a reminder, what the first verse in it established, in the most complete manner, with an added warning. So the last connected to the first and joined with it in the best and most beautiful connection, and it looked to the beginning of "al-Zumar" in the greatest and most complete look. So how excellent is this arrangement! By my life, it is brighter than the sun at forenoon and more complete than the full moon. Glory be to Him who sent it down, made it beautiful, detailed it, favored it, ennobled it, and honored it. And God knows best.
